title: Spring Boot configuration validation: reject an unusable relay before work starts
summary: Validated configuration prevents a Spring Boot context from starting with a batch size outside the declared operating range.
body:
Validated configuration prevents a Spring Boot context from starting with a batch size outside the declared operating range.

Fail at binding

The RelaySettings record carries @Min(1), @Max(100) and @NotNull constraints. The test passes --relay.batch-size=0 over a valid default. Context creation throws a runtime startup failure; the failure analysis names the command-line property origin and the minimum constraint. No scheduler starts in this small configuration context.

The test checks the invalid effective value, not a controller request. A bad setting should fail before the worker claims events. The precedence lesson explains how the invalid command-line value wins. Existing configuration material covers typed binding more generally.

What one constraint misses

Min and max protect only the numeric range. They do not prove that batch size 100 fits connection-pool capacity, that timeout matches a service objective, or that a secret points to a trusted endpoint. Validate cross-field invariants where needed and exercise them in a startup test. Keep the error message useful without printing a secret value.

The fixture has no external database or broker. A successfully bound configuration does not mean dependencies are ready. Readiness is a separate operational signal after startup.

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties("relay")
record RelaySettings(@Min(1) @Max(100) int batchSize,
                     @NotNull Duration timeout) { }

  • Do not treat successful binding as dependency readiness.
  • Do not leak secret values in startup errors.

title: Spring Boot configuration sources: test each deployment path, not a guessed order
summary: A configuration source matrix records which value reaches a typed bean when defaults, files, environment variables and command-line arguments disagree.
body:
A configuration source matrix records which value reaches a typed bean when defaults, files, environment variables and command-line arguments disagree.

Two forms of evidence

The kit has an ApplicationContextRunner test that inserts a packaged-default source and an operator source manually, then checks the bound timeout. A newer SpringApplicationBuilder test passes defaults and a command-line override through Boot startup. Both checks are narrow. The newer BootRelaySettingsTest also reads a real local temporary application.properties file. RelaySettingsProcessTest now sets real child-process environment values and reads local relative config imports. A synthetic local configtree is now checked in a child process. A deployment-mounted file and secret source remain untested.

Build a deployment matrix with one case per actual source combination: packaged file, profile-specific file, mounted file, environment variable, command-line flag and secret store. Assert the effective bean value and the source origin for a non-secret key. The CLI check is the first checked row. The manual source check is a second, different row.

Reduce configuration drift

Use one prefix and document the supported keys. A property name that changes between releases needs a migration notice and a test for the old key. Fail startup when a required setting is absent. Unknown fields require a policy: Boot binding can ignore unknown names unless the application opts into stricter behavior, so a typo may leave the default running.

Do not publish values for credentials. Verify that a secret is present and correctly shaped without returning it in an error page or health detail. A deployment-specific override deserves a real startup test in the deployment environment, not only a unit test with a MapPropertySource.

Checked source

// Matrix to add outside this kit:
// packaged file × profile file × environment × CLI × mounted secret
// Assert the bound RelaySettings value for each supported combination.

Verification boundary

ConfigurationOverrideBoundaryTest.selectsAndValidatesTheEffectiveTimeout and BootRelaySettingsTest.commandLineOverridesPackagedDefaults. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

The full matrix is a plan. A manual two-source override, Boot default/CLI override, local additional file and file/CLI collision are checked. A selected review profile and missing required/optional imports are also checked. Host environment variables and mounted deployment files remain untested.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not claim a real environment-variable test from a manually inserted MapPropertySource.
  • Do not display secret values when explaining origin.
  • Do not assume a misspelled property causes startup failure by default.

title: Spring database rollout: add a nullable column before changing every writer
summary: An expand migration adds schema capacity while the old application version can still write rows.
body:
An expand migration adds schema capacity while the old application version can still write rows.

The checked expansion

SchemaEvolutionContractTest starts with receipt_id and amount_minor, then adds nullable tenant_id. It inserts an old-shape row that names only the original columns. H2 accepts the row, leaving tenant_id null. This proves the local expansion preserves old-writer compatibility for that one insert shape.

The fixture then backfills both existing rows to legacy. The backfill lesson explains why a production update needs batches and a tenant ownership rule. The Java migration page describes versioned application boundaries; this Spring page focuses on the datasource behavior in the kit.

Roll forward in stages

A deployed sequence usually needs: add a nullable column, deploy code that writes it, backfill historical rows, verify absence of nulls, then add a required constraint. If old instances remain during a rolling release, contracting early breaks them. The test demonstrates exactly that rejection in the contract phase.

H2 DDL and production DDL differ. Large table rewrites, lock duration, replication lag and rollback rules need target-database tests. The source kit invokes SQL directly; it does not run a migration tool or store a schema history.

Checked source

alter table shipment_receipt add column tenant_id varchar(40);
insert into shipment_receipt(receipt_id, amount_minor) values (102, 500);

Verification boundary

SchemaEvolutionContractTest.nullableExpansionAcceptsOldWriterAndBackfillPreservesRows. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

One H2 table and two rows are checked. No rolling deployment, target-database lock estimate or versioned migration runner is present.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not add NOT NULL before old writers are gone or updated.
  • Do not use select-star assumptions across a schema rollout.
  • Do not treat H2 DDL cost as a production estimate.

title: Spring database backfill: assign historical rows before enforcing ownership
summary: A backfill assigns a valid tenant value to historical rows while a new column is still nullable.
body:
A backfill assigns a valid tenant value to historical rows while a new column is still nullable.

The checked row state

The H2 fixture inserts one row before expansion and one old-writer row afterward. Both have null tenant_id until an UPDATE assigns legacy. A count then finds two legacy rows. This is an explicit local rule chosen for the fixture; it is not a safe universal rule for assigning real customer records.

For a real tenant migration, derive ownership from trusted existing data. Quarantine rows whose owner cannot be proven. Count unresolved rows before adding a NOT NULL constraint. Tenant predicates only protect reads once the stored owner is correct; a wrong backfill can make authorization consistently wrong.

Bound the production job

The fixture updates the entire tiny table in one statement. On a large table, choose bounded batches with a stable key range or cursor, record progress, make reruns idempotent and monitor lock waits. A process can fail between batches; restarting should not duplicate or skip work. Verify sample rows and total counts before contraction.

A migration tool can version the DDL, but a data backfill may need a separate controlled job and audit trail. The runner lesson states what this kit does not automate. The contract test shows the failure old writers see after the final constraint.

Checked source

update shipment_receipt
set tenant_id = 'legacy'
where tenant_id is null;

Verification boundary

SchemaEvolutionContractTest.nullableExpansionAcceptsOldWriterAndBackfillPreservesRows. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

The test has two rows and a single H2 UPDATE. It does not prove correct ownership of real tenant data, bounded lock time or restart-safe batch progress.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not invent a tenant owner for ambiguous historical data.
  • Do not run an unbounded update on a large table without measuring locks.
  • Do not enforce NOT NULL while unresolved rows remain.

title: Spring database contract phase: reject old writers only after backfill
summary: A contract migration enforces a required tenant column after data and application writers have moved to the new shape.
body:
A contract migration enforces a required tenant column after data and application writers have moved to the new shape.

The checked boundary

The test adds tenant_id as nullable, backfills the original row, then sets the column NOT NULL. An old writer that inserts only receipt_id and amount_minor now fails with a translated data-integrity exception. A new writer that supplies tenant_id=east succeeds. Two rows remain after the rejected insert.

That failure is the point of the test. The expansion phase lets both writer shapes coexist; the contract phase deliberately ends old-writer compatibility. Expansion and backfill must be verified before this step reaches a rolling deployment.

Gate on observed state

Before contraction, check that all running application versions write the new column, unresolved null count is zero, backfill ownership has been reviewed and rollback plans do not require the old writer. Keep the migration step in version control and test it on the target engine. H2 accepts this DDL, but its locks and failure modes are not a production model.

The local test starts from a new in-memory database each run. It does not prove that applying a migration twice is safe, that a mixed-version fleet has drained, or that a failed production DDL transaction rolls back. Migration tooling needs separate integration checks.

Checked source

alter table shipment_receipt alter column tenant_id set not null;
-- Old insert omitting tenant_id now fails.
insert into shipment_receipt(receipt_id, amount_minor, tenant_id)
values (103, 900, 'east');

Verification boundary

SchemaEvolutionContractTest.contractRejectsOldWriterOnlyAfterBackfill. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

The test checks one H2 constraint transition. It does not run a mixed-version service fleet, a target database or a migration history runner.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not contract before old writers stop.
  • Do not assume failed production DDL rolls back as H2 does.
  • Do not skip the null-count and ownership checks.

title: Spring Boot migrations: what a versioned runner must add to the SQL test
summary: A versioned migration runner records which schema changes have been applied so application startup and deployment can reason about database state.
body:
A versioned migration runner records which schema changes have been applied so application startup and deployment can reason about database state.

The current kit boundary

SchemaEvolutionContractTest calls JdbcTemplate.execute with ALTER TABLE statements and uses a fresh H2 database for each test. It checks the row behavior of expand, backfill and contract. A separate FlywayReceiptMigrationTest now executes three test-only versioned SQL files, records history and checks validation. SchemaEvolutionContractTest remains direct SQL; no runtime migration-on-startup wiring, target-engine test or repair policy is included.

Spring Boot can invoke a migration tool when the tool and its integration are present. A production rollout should pin migration scripts in version control, apply each version once, verify checksums and test the same scripts on the target database. The expansion fixture supplies a small SQL contract, not that deployment workflow.

Separate DDL from long data work

A backfill of millions of rows may exceed startup time and lock budgets. Keep it resumable and observable rather than hiding it in a startup hook. Gate contraction on measured completion and on old-writer retirement. Specify whether the migration runner or deployment pipeline owns execution so two rollout processes do not race ambiguously.

The next integration test should start from the previous released schema, apply versioned scripts, start old and new writers at the right stages, and inspect history plus row state after a failure. The test matrix names those cases.

Checked source

// The following names are a sketch; checked files are under db/relay-migration:
// V1__create_shipment_receipt.sql
// V2__add_nullable_tenant_id.sql
// V3__require_tenant_id.sql

Verification boundary

SchemaEvolutionContractTest checks direct H2 SQL. FlywayReceiptMigrationTest checks direct test-scoped Flyway execution and history; BootFlywayStartupTest checks a separate Boot context. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

Migration history and checksum validation are now checked in a separate H2 fixture. Target-database DDL, concurrent deployment, ReceiptApplication runtime integration and rollback remain untested. A separate non-web Boot startup test covers the local H2 migration path. The names above are a sketch; the actual test files have different names.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call direct JdbcTemplate DDL a versioned Flyway migration.
  • Do not place an unbounded backfill in application startup.
  • Do not contract before application versions and data are ready.

title: Spring schema rollout tests: check old and new writers at every phase
summary: A schema rollout test matrix runs the old and new application write shapes against each migration phase.
body:
A schema rollout test matrix runs the old and new application write shapes against each migration phase.

The local assertions

The source kit checks two points. After nullable expansion, an old insert omitting tenant_id succeeds and the backfill assigns both rows. After NOT NULL contraction, that old insert fails and a new insert with tenant_id succeeds. The tests inspect counts and stored values, not only exception types.

That is a useful local contract, but a production sequence has more states: old code on old schema, old code on expanded schema, new code on expanded schema, new code after backfill and new code on contracted schema. The first fixture and the second cover only a small subset in H2.

Move to the target engine

Run the exact versioned SQL against the production database engine in a disposable integration environment. Include realistic indexes and row counts, concurrent traffic, migration restart after failure, read replicas if used and DDL lock monitoring. Check that rollback to the previous application version is possible at each deployment stage; after contraction it may not be.

Do not infer Flyway history behavior from the direct JdbcTemplate tests; a separate FlywayReceiptMigrationTest now checks it on H2. The runner plan is separate. Keep a reviewer-visible record of which versions can coexist.

title: Spring exercise: predict startup and SQL states across a staged rollout
summary: A rollout trace asks which configuration value binds and which write shape survives each database phase.
body:
A rollout trace asks which configuration value binds and which write shape survives each database phase.

Resolve startup first

The application default says relay.batch-size=8 and relay.timeout=2s. The operator passes --relay.batch-size=12 and --relay.timeout=450ms. Predict the bound record: batch size 12, timeout 450 milliseconds. Change the batch flag to 0; startup fails before a worker can claim an event. These are checked by BootRelaySettingsTest.

Now add nullable tenant_id to shipment_receipt. An old writer omitting it succeeds. Backfill historical rows to legacy. Set tenant_id NOT NULL. The same old insert fails; a writer supplying east succeeds. These states are checked by SchemaEvolutionContractTest. The contract lesson explains why an old version must be drained first.

Change the rollout

Suppose ten million rows have no trusted tenant owner. Do not label all of them legacy merely to satisfy a constraint. Describe how to quarantine ambiguous rows, batch provable assignments and measure completion. Then write the target-database and versioned-runner tests still missing from the kit.

The exercise combines separate local fixtures. It is not a deployed migration, hosted judge or authorization audit. The configuration matrix and the schema matrix are the next checks.

title: Spring Boot external config file: bind the value the process actually loads
summary: An additional configuration location adds a properties file to Spring Boot startup before a typed configuration bean is bound.
body:
An additional configuration location adds a properties file to Spring Boot startup before a typed configuration bean is bound.

Load a real file

BootRelaySettingsTest writes application.properties into a JUnit temporary directory. It starts a non-web SpringApplication context with spring.config.additional-location set to that directory URI. The file supplies relay.batch-size=17 and relay.timeout=750ms; the bound RelaySettings record reports those values instead of the programmatic defaults of 8 and 2s. This is a real file read, not a MapPropertySource inserted after startup.

Boot resolves additional locations early. A directory URI needs its trailing separator so the loader can look for application.properties inside it. The test obtains that URI from Path.toUri rather than joining a platform-specific path string. The source matrix now has a checked file row, but a mounted volume with different permissions still needs a deployment test.

Keep the file operationally boring

Store only non-secret relay settings in the example file. A mounted secret needs access controls, rotation and an error policy that does not print its value. Treat a missing additional location as a startup or rollout decision; do not silently assume the intended file was read just because the application starts with defaults.

The startup validator checks value ranges after binding. It cannot tell whether a plausible value came from the intended source. An effective-settings diagnostic can report selected non-secret values and their origins to operators, while omitting credentials.

Checked source

Files.writeString(configDirectory.resolve("application.properties"),
    "relay.batch-size=17\nrelay.timeout=750ms\n");
try (var context = app().run(
    "--spring.config.additional-location=" + configDirectory.toUri())) {
    assertEquals(17, context.getBean(RelaySettings.class).batchSize());
}

Verification boundary

BootRelaySettingsTest.additionalPropertiesFileOverridesPackagedDefaults. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

The test uses one local temporary file and one process. It does not exercise containers, permissions on a production mount, a remote secret store or profile-specific file selection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not append a filename where Boot expects a directory location.
  • Do not infer that a missing config file was loaded from a plausible default value.
  • Do not log credentials while reporting effective settings.

title: Spring Boot file versus command line: assert the bound result
summary: When a command-line argument and an additional properties file set the same key, the effective value reaches the bound bean from the command line in this fixture.
body:
When a command-line argument and an additional properties file set the same key, the effective value reaches the bound bean from the command line in this fixture.

The collision test

The temporary file sets relay.batch-size=17 and relay.timeout=750ms. The application starts with --relay.batch-size=23. BootRelaySettingsTest asserts batchSize 23 and timeout 750 milliseconds on RelaySettings. Checking both fields matters: a mistaken global replacement could make the first assertion pass while discarding the file entirely.

This proves the ordering of the two sources in the checked Boot 4.0.8 startup path. It does not establish the ordering of every environment variable, imported location or platform secret. The file-only test isolates loading. The default-versus-CLI test isolates the older, narrower collision.

Report the effective value

A runbook that lists a value in application.properties but ignores launch arguments can describe the wrong worker capacity. Read the bound settings at startup or through a protected diagnostic endpoint. Redact secrets and retain the property origin only where operators need it.

For a poller, changing batch size changes database query work, heap allocation and per-tick duration. That is an operational choice, not only a syntax question. The polling budget explains the load consequence.

Checked source

try (var context = app().run(
    "--spring.config.additional-location=" + configDirectory.toUri(),
    "--relay.batch-size=23")) {
    var settings = context.getBean(RelaySettings.class);
    assertEquals(23, settings.batchSize());
    assertEquals(Duration.ofMillis(750), settings.timeout());
}

Verification boundary

Costs and limits

The test checks a local file and CLI against programmatic defaults. It does not set a real operating-system environment variable or exercise cloud configuration injection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not compare only raw Environment strings when callers use typed configuration beans.
  • Do not assume one overridden key replaces every key from the file.
  • Do not promote a test batch size into a production capacity recommendation.

title: Spring Boot config validation: separate valid syntax from a safe relay setting
summary: Configuration binding converts external text into a typed setting; validation then rejects a value outside the application contract.
body:
Configuration binding converts external text into a typed setting; validation then rejects a value outside the application contract.

Two separate failures

The RelaySettings record binds an int batchSize and a Duration timeout. Its batch size has a 1..100 constraint. A command-line value of zero causes context startup to fail; the test asserts failure rather than allowing a worker to run with no useful batch. A file containing 750ms binds Duration.ofMillis(750), which avoids an implicit unit guess.

The file tests check only accepted values. They do not yet test a corrupt file, a missing required key when a programmatic default is removed, an unknown property or a secret source outage. File loading and precedence happen before the final bean is judged.

Treat a restart as a configuration change

A 100-row upper bound is a validity guard, not a load-test result. The service can still overload a small database with a value inside the allowed range. Roll out a changed batch size with queue-age, connection-wait and tick-duration observations. If the value is rejected, the process should remain unready rather than starting a worker with a guessed fallback.

Config values must not appear in failure reports when they are credentials. Keep the typed bean small and avoid using a secret as an exception message. Readiness checks apply once startup succeeds; they do not repair a failed bind.

Checked source

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties("relay")
record RelaySettings(@Min(1) @Max(100) int batchSize,
                     @NotNull Duration timeout) { }
assertThrows(RuntimeException.class,
    () -> app().run("--relay.batch-size=0"));

Verification boundary

Costs and limits

The fixture checks one invalid integer and explicit Duration units. It does not prove every configuration key, secret source, mount failure or operational capacity limit.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not confuse a parseable value with an acceptable operating point.
  • Do not silently replace an invalid operator value with a default.
  • Do not expose secret values in binding diagnostics.

title: Flyway SQL migrations: record ordered schema changes against a real database
summary: A versioned Flyway migration applies a named SQL file once and records its outcome in a schema-history table.
body:
A versioned Flyway migration applies a named SQL file once and records its outcome in a schema-history table.

The checked sequence

The source kit ships V1__create_receipts.sql, V2__expand_tenant.sql and V3__backfill_and_contract.sql under a test-only migration location. FlywayReceiptMigrationTest applies versions 1, 2 and 3 in separate steps against one H2 database. It asserts one executed migration at each step, three successful versioned history entries after version 3 and zero new executions on a second migrate call.

The test configures Flyway through its Java API. The dependency is test-scoped; the downloadable application does not run migrations on production startup. The older runner-boundary lesson now points to this checked fixture. Boot integration remains an explicit deployment choice.

Own the files, not just the final schema

Changing a SQL file after it has been applied changes what the version claims to mean. Commit migration files with the application change and review the old application against every intermediate schema. A migration version is not a license to skip the compatibility interval.

The first file creates one receipt table and a seed row. That seed is fixture data, not a recommendation to store business seed records in every production migration. Keep a separate procedure for large data backfills and target-engine DDL planning.

Checked source

Flyway.configure().dataSource(source)
    .locations("classpath:db/relay-migration").target("2").load().migrate();
// The test then runs the old insert while tenant_id is nullable.

Verification boundary

FlywayReceiptMigrationTest.orderedFilesPreserveTheOldWriterUntilContract. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

Flyway runs through its Java API on H2 2.3.232. This is not a Spring Boot auto-configuration test or a deployment against PostgreSQL, MySQL or another production engine.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call direct ALTER TABLE tests migration-history tests.
  • Do not edit an applied versioned file as a normal repair.
  • Do not place an unbounded production backfill in application startup.

title: Flyway expand and contract: show exactly when an old writer breaks
summary: An expand-and-contract rollout keeps old writes valid while a new nullable column is introduced, then rejects them only after the constraint is tightened.
body:
An expand-and-contract rollout keeps old writes valid while a new nullable column is introduced, then rejects them only after the constraint is tightened.

Version 2 is the overlap window

V1 creates shipment_receipt with receipt_id and amount_minor. V2 adds nullable tenant_id. After Flyway applies V2, the test inserts receipt 102 without tenant_id; both the seed and new row have null tenant_id. That is intentional. The old writer still runs, so a new reader must not assume every historical row has an owner.

V3 assigns legacy to the null rows and then sets tenant_id NOT NULL. The test checks that no null rows remain, the old insert fails and a new insert with tenant_id=east succeeds. The direct SQL expansion check and the constraint lesson explain each phase without migration tooling.

The fixture is smaller than a deployment

The test performs a backfill and NOT NULL alteration in one tiny H2 migration. A large production table may require resumable batches, index planning and an application release between backfill and constraint. New writers should deploy before V3 and old writers should retire before V3. The fixture checks SQL behavior, not that rollout timing.

When two application versions coexist, tenant-scoped reads need a policy for still-null rows. Guessing the tenant from a default can make authorization consistently wrong. The tenant predicate shows why ownership must be established before scoped queries trust it.

Checked source

-- V2__expand_tenant.sql
alter table shipment_receipt add column tenant_id varchar(40);
-- V3__backfill_and_contract.sql
update shipment_receipt set tenant_id = 'legacy' where tenant_id is null;
alter table shipment_receipt alter column tenant_id set not null;

Verification boundary

FlywayReceiptMigrationTest.orderedFilesPreserveTheOldWriterUntilContract. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

Two rows and one H2 process do not measure lock time, batch cost, data ownership accuracy, mixed-version processes or recovery from an interrupted migration.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not require the new column in the same step that introduces it to an old writer.
  • Do not assign a guessed tenant to production records.
  • Do not infer target-engine DDL lock behavior from H2.

title: Flyway validation: detect a changed applied migration before another write
summary: Flyway validation compares discovered migration definitions with the recorded history for already applied versions.
body:
Flyway validation compares discovered migration definitions with the recorded history for already applied versions.

The ordinary path

After applying V1 through V3, the fixture counts three successful versioned history entries, reruns migrate and sees zero executed migrations, then calls validate without failure. The check is about history consistency, not business-row correctness. The receipt assertions separately prove that the column contract changed as expected.

A second test deliberately corrupts the recorded checksum for version 2 and expects FlywayValidateException. That is a controlled simulation of a history mismatch. It does not edit a committed migration file or show how an operator should repair a production history table. The versioned-file lesson establishes the files being compared.

Do not auto-repair uncertainty

A mismatch is a reason to stop and inspect the deployed file, prior release artifact and schema state. Rewriting history to silence validation can hide drift. A failed non-transactional DDL step needs a database-specific recovery procedure, a reviewed forward migration or a restore decision.

The fixture is isolated H2 and has no concurrent migrators. It does not show a process crash between SQL statements, target-database transaction semantics or deployment locks. The rollout matrix lists the untested states.

Checked source

migrationAt("3").migrate();
jdbc.update("update "flyway_schema_history" "
    + "set "checksum" = "checksum" + 1 where "version" = '2'");
assertThrows(FlywayValidateException.class,
    () -> migrationAt("3").validate());

Verification boundary

FlywayReceiptMigrationTest.changedRecordedChecksumFailsValidation. The excerpt is shortened or a labelled design sketch; the kit contains the checked tests.

Costs and limits

The test corrupts a checksum in an isolated H2 history table. It does not change a deployed SQL file, perform repair or prove crash recovery for DDL on another engine.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a green row-count check as migration-history validation.
  • Do not change recorded checksums manually in a deployed database to clear an error.
  • Do not assume every database rolls back DDL on migration failure.

title: Spring Boot and Flyway: choose who runs migrations before traffic starts
summary: Spring Boot can invoke Flyway migrations during application startup when the runtime dependency and database are configured.
body:
Spring Boot can invoke Flyway migrations during application startup when the runtime dependency and database are configured.

What this kit actually does

The downloadable kit now declares spring-boot-starter-flyway with test scope. FlywayReceiptMigrationTest creates a Flyway instance directly; BootFlywayStartupTest also checks a separate non-web Boot context. ReceiptApplication still does not enable a runtime migration path. The generated SQL files sit under db/relay-migration, away from Boot’s conventional db/migration path. This separation keeps a reader from mistaking a checked teaching fixture for a production rollout.

If an application startup owns migrations, coordinate concurrent replicas and readiness so none serves a schema it cannot read. If a deployment job owns them, make the job idempotent and gate the rollout on its result. Choose one owner. The API test proves ordered local execution, not either deployment arrangement.

Match dependency scope to ownership

Moving Flyway to runtime and placing scripts in the configured location is a deliberate application change. The target database may need an additional Flyway database module. Run the exact scripts against a disposable instance of that engine before promotion. Test old and new application versions across V2; after V3 the old writer is intentionally incompatible.

Never start a long, unbounded data backfill on every replica. A migration tool records versions; it does not decide business ownership for historical rows or guarantee zero lock time. The staged rollout names those decisions.

Checked source

<!-- The source kit keeps this test-only. Runtime rollout requires an owner. -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-flyway</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

A separate non-web Boot auto-configuration test now checks local startup on H2. No production database module, concurrent-replica deployment job, readiness gate or target-engine migration is checked.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a test-scoped dependency production migration wiring.
  • Do not let both a job and every replica own the same rollout without a deliberate coordination plan.
  • Do not assume migration history proves the application can read all legacy rows.

title: Spring exercise: predict file overrides and three migration versions
summary: A release trace records the bound worker settings and the receipt writes that remain legal at each migration version.
body:
A release trace records the bound worker settings and the receipt writes that remain legal at each migration version.

Settings trace

Start with programmatic defaults batchSize=8 and timeout=2s. Add a file with batchSize=17 and timeout=750ms. The bound record becomes 17 and 750ms. Add the command-line argument --relay.batch-size=23. The bound record becomes 23 and 750ms. The two BootRelaySettingsTest file cases check those exact states. Replace the command-line value with zero and startup fails validation.

For each state, write the effective value, its source and whether a worker may start. Do not infer that an absent mounted file was read from the presence of an acceptable default. The collision lesson explains the checked row.

Database trace

At V1, tenant_id does not exist. At V2, the old insert omitting tenant_id succeeds and leaves null. At V3, migration backfills existing null rows and requires tenant_id on future inserts. The old insert then fails; a new insert with east succeeds. Record the count of applied versions as 1, 2 and 3. A repeated migrate at V3 executes zero files.

Now change the recorded checksum for V2 in a disposable test database and run validate. Expect a validation exception before another release proceeds. Explain why rewriting history is not the repair plan. Run the named Maven tests and compare your trace with their assertions; the exercise has no hosted judge.

Checked source

mvn -q -Dtest=BootRelaySettingsTest,FlywayReceiptMigrationTest test

Verification boundary

Costs and limits

The trace uses a local file and H2 migrations. It does not prove mounted-secret behavior, target-engine DDL, mixed-version deployment timing or recovery after a process kill.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not carry the file batch size through a later command-line override.
  • Do not expect an old writer to work after V3 requires tenant_id.
  • Do not describe a checksum mismatch as a row-data error.

title: Spring Boot profile files: bind only the selected environment override
summary: A profile-specific properties file contributes settings when its named Spring profile is active.
body:
A profile-specific properties file contributes settings when its named Spring profile is active.

The checked choice

BootRelaySettingsTest writes two files into a temporary directory. application.properties sets batch size 17 and timeout 750ms. application-review.properties sets batch size 29 only. The context starts with review active and the additional directory selected. The bound RelaySettings record reports 29 and 750ms. The profile file overrides one key; the base file still supplies the other.

The selected value matters to a background worker. A team can inspect the base file and assume 17 rows per tick while the deployed profile actually admits 29. The CLI collision test shows a further override. The polling budget explains why a larger batch needs load measurements.

Do not treat profile names as access control

A profile selects configuration. It does not authenticate a caller, hide a secret or prevent an operator from starting the wrong profile. Print the active profile and non-secret effective settings in a protected startup diagnostic. Check a real deployment with its selected file; this fixture uses local JUnit files.

If two profiles define the same key, define and test their order for that deployment. This test selects one profile and does not claim every multi-profile ordering rule. A required setting should still be validated after all selected sources are loaded.

Checked source

Files.writeString(dir.resolve("application.properties"),
    "relay.batch-size=17\nrelay.timeout=750ms\n");
Files.writeString(dir.resolve("application-review.properties"),
    "relay.batch-size=29\n");
try (var context = app().run("--spring.profiles.active=review",
    "--spring.config.additional-location=" + dir.toUri())) {
    assertEquals(29, context.getBean(RelaySettings.class).batchSize());
}

Verification boundary

BootRelaySettingsTest.activeProfileLoadsItsFileOverTheBaseFile. The excerpt is shortened; the source kit contains the checked fixture.

Costs and limits

Only one local profile and a JUnit temporary directory are checked. No container mount, process environment variable, secret store or multi-profile collision is exercised.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not read only the base file when a profile is active.
  • Do not assume a profile is an authorization boundary.
  • Do not size production batches from one local fixture.

title: Spring Boot config import: fail startup when a required file is missing
summary: A non-optional config import makes a missing external file a startup error rather than an unnoticed fallback.
body:
A non-optional config import makes a missing external file a startup error rather than an unnoticed fallback.

The missing-file test

BootRelaySettingsTest points spring.config.import at a file URI that does not exist. The non-web Boot context fails before a RelaySettings bean can run. The test does not assert a specific outer exception class because Boot wraps the missing-location cause while constructing the application.

This policy fits a setting that must come from deployment state. If the application silently falls back to an old batch size or stale endpoint, it may process work with the wrong assumptions. The optional case deliberately chooses different behavior. Document which imports are mandatory and check that the intended path is mounted before rollout.

Do not put secrets into diagnostics

A location error may reveal the path, while binding errors can reveal a rejected value. Avoid putting credentials in command-line arguments or startup logs. A missing secret import should prevent a service from accepting traffic, but the error page should not include a credential.

The test proves a missing local file is rejected. It does not verify a readable file that contains a wrong key, wrong permissions, a rotated secret, or the availability of a remote configuration service. Typed validation handles the value after a source is loaded.

String missing = configDirectory.resolve("missing.properties").toUri().toString();

title: Spring Boot optional config import: know which default survives
summary: An optional config import lets startup proceed when its file is absent, leaving other configuration sources to supply the effective value.
body:
An optional config import lets startup proceed when its file is absent, leaving other configuration sources to supply the effective value.

The checked fallback

BootRelaySettingsTest prefixes an absent file URI with optional:. The context starts and RelaySettings reports the declared defaults: batch size 8 and timeout 2s. Those values are not proof that the file was loaded. The test chooses absence on purpose and asserts the fallback state.

For a local developer override, optional behavior can be useful. For a production-required endpoint or credential, it can hide a broken mount. The required import makes that failure visible. Decide per setting; do not apply optional: to an entire configuration path as a reflex.

Make a fallback observable

An operator should be able to tell whether the optional source was present without exposing secret values. Report a source-availability signal or a redacted effective setting. If the default is unsafe for production, reject startup with typed validation or a deployment-specific requirement.

This fixture has one absent file and programmatic defaults. It does not test partially written files, permission errors or simultaneous environment and CLI overrides. The source matrix separates those combinations.

Checked source

String missing = configDirectory.resolve("missing.properties").toUri().toString();
try (var context = app().run(
    "--spring.config.import=optional:" + missing)) {
    assertEquals(8, context.getBean(RelaySettings.class).batchSize());
}

Verification boundary

Costs and limits

The fallback is checked for one local missing file. It does not establish that any other optional source is safe to omit in production.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not interpret a valid default as evidence that an import succeeded.
  • Do not make a required secret optional.
  • Do not hide the source of an effective value from operators.

summary: A programmatic SpringApplication default has lower priority than configuration loaded from the application file in this checked startup path.

A programmatic SpringApplication default has lower priority than configuration loaded from the application file in this checked startup path.

A test that first used the wrong database

The source kit packages spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:receipt_application. The first BootFlywayStartupTest supplied a unique H2 URL with SpringApplicationBuilder.properties. Boot still opened the packaged receipt_application database. Two test stages therefore touched the wrong shared database, and a supposed checksum failure did not occur. The test was corrected to pass the unique URL as a command-line argument.

This is a concrete reason to inspect the effective DataSource, not just a builder call. The settings fixture checks that CLI values reach a bound bean. The migration fixture now checks separate database histories across two context starts.

Protect isolation

A test URL that is accidentally shadowed can contaminate another test or make a migration appear repeatable for the wrong reason. Use an isolated database name, assert the expected schema history and inspect the connection URL when setup is ambiguous. Do not rely on tests passing in one fixed order.

The source kit uses H2 with DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1 so two contexts can see the same named database during one test. That is deliberate for the V2-to-V3 trace. It is not a persistence guarantee across process restarts.

    .web(WebApplicationType.NONE)
    .properties("spring.flyway.locations=classpath:db/relay-migration")
    .run("--spring.datasource.url=" + uniqueH2Url);

title: Spring Boot Flyway startup: apply versioned SQL before querying a receipt
summary: Spring Boot can create a Flyway bean and migrate the configured DataSource while its application context starts.
body:
Spring Boot can create a Flyway bean and migrate the configured DataSource while its application context starts.

The checked non-web context

BootFlywayStartupTest starts a minimal non-web Boot context with the test-scoped spring-boot-starter-flyway. It points spring.flyway.locations at three SQL resources under db/relay-migration and selects target version 2. When run returns, the test obtains Flyway and JdbcTemplate beans and counts two versioned history entries. The old receipt insert then succeeds while tenant_id is nullable.

A second context starts against the same named H2 database with target version 3. Boot applies the remaining migration before the test reads rows. The older insert shape now fails the NOT NULL constraint; the new shape succeeds. The SQL phase lesson explains why this is a compatibility interval rather than a single schema flip.

Name the application boundary

This test proves Boot auto-configuration in a separate test application. It does not wire Flyway into the runnable ReceiptApplication. The starter is test-scoped, and the migrations are test resources. The ownership decision remains open for a real rollout.

H2 2.3.232 checks the local sequence. It does not measure DDL locks, transaction behavior or a concurrent replica deployment on the target engine. The startup path must be tested again against that engine before a production release.

Checked source

try (var context = start(uniqueH2Url, 2)) {
    assertNotNull(context.getBean(Flyway.class));
    var jdbc = context.getBean(JdbcTemplate.class);
    jdbc.update("insert into shipment_receipt(receipt_id, amount_minor) values (102, 500)");
}

  • Do not put the contract migration into service before old writers retire.

title: Spring Boot migration target: test an old writer before closing the schema
summary: A staged migration test can stop at an intermediate version to check whether an older application write remains valid.
body:
A staged migration test can stop at an intermediate version to check whether an older application write remains valid.

V2 accepts the old shape

The first Boot context targets migration version 2. Its receipt table has a nullable tenant_id. The test inserts receipt 102 with only receipt_id and amount_minor. Both that row and the V1 seed row have null tenant_id. A new reader that assumes ownership is already populated would be wrong during this overlap.

The second context targets version 3 against the same H2 URL. Flyway backfills those rows and tightens tenant_id to NOT NULL. The test counts zero null owners and rejects an old-shape insert. It then accepts receipt 104 with east as tenant. The contract phase must follow an application rollout that already writes the new field.

This is a version step, not live coexistence

The test closes the first context before opening the second. It does not run old and new processes at the same time. A real release should start both versions against a disposable target-engine database while traffic continues, then verify reads, writes and rollback options at each version.

V3 backfills a tiny test table in one statement. A large table may need bounded, resumable work with business-reviewed tenant assignment. A NOT NULL constraint can enforce presence, not correctness of that assignment.

Checked source

spring.flyway.target=2
# Old write omitting tenant_id succeeds here.
spring.flyway.target=3
# Only the new write shape succeeds after this stage.

Costs and limits

Two contexts run sequentially on H2. There is no simultaneous old/new process pair, real user traffic or target-engine DDL measurement.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not deploy the NOT NULL phase while an old writer still runs.
  • Do not label a sequential test a mixed-version concurrency test.
  • Do not equate a non-null legacy value with verified tenant ownership.

title: Spring Boot migration history failure: stop context startup on a mismatch
summary: A changed recorded migration checksum can prevent a Boot context from completing startup when Flyway validates history.
body:
A changed recorded migration checksum can prevent a Boot context from completing startup when Flyway validates history.

The isolated failure

BootFlywayStartupTest first starts at version 3 in an isolated H2 database. It then changes the recorded checksum for V2 in that disposable history table and closes the context. A second Boot start against the same database throws before returning an application context. The test asserts failure; it does not suppress the mismatch or call repair.

The direct API fixture isolates the validation exception. This Boot fixture checks the additional boundary: the application context itself does not finish creation. A deployment platform should keep an instance out of traffic when startup fails, but that platform behavior is not exercised here.

Stop and inspect before repair

A checksum mismatch may mean an applied file changed, an artifact was built incorrectly or the history table was altered. Inspect the release artifact and actual schema before deciding on a forward migration or a database-specific recovery procedure. Editing the history row to make startup pass can hide incompatible state.

The test deliberately modifies a checksum, not a SQL file. It says nothing about incomplete DDL on engines that cannot roll back a failed migration. The test-scope boundary also means ReceiptApplication has no such startup gate yet.

Checked source

try (var context = start(url, 3)) {
    context.getBean(JdbcTemplate.class).update(
        "update "flyway_schema_history" set "checksum" = "checksum" + 1 where "version" = '2'");
}
assertThrows(RuntimeException.class, () -> start(url, 3));

Verification boundary

BootFlywayStartupTest.invalidHistoryPreventsTheNextBootStartup. The excerpt is shortened; the source kit contains the checked fixture.

Costs and limits

The mismatch is injected into H2 history. No applied SQL file is edited and no deployment orchestrator, target engine or recovery action is tested.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not clear a checksum error by rewriting production history without investigation.
  • Do not serve traffic from a context that failed startup.
  • Do not treat a checksum check as proof that business rows are correct.

Configuration trace

A versioned receipt project should prove schema transitions before promoting a database-backed API.

Assemble the local check

The source kit already has three migration files and a non-web Boot startup fixture. Run V2, insert an old-shape receipt, then run V3 against the same named H2 database. Check history, backfilled rows, old-writer rejection and new-writer acceptance. Run a separate checksum-mismatch test to confirm startup fails rather than serving against uncertain schema state.

This is a project boundary, not a deployed receipt service. ReceiptApplication still uses an in-memory ReceiptStore and fixture Basic authentication. The test starter and SQL resources are not runtime migration wiring. The earlier API project describes that runnable surface; the test-scope lesson marks what remains separate.

Choose the next release gate

Decide whether an application instance or a deployment job owns migrations. Use a disposable instance of the selected production database, not H2 alone. Start actual old and new application versions across V2; measure DDL locks and verify rollback options. Backfill tenant ownership from an authoritative source before enforcing NOT NULL.

Only after those checks should the API use a persistent repository and make readiness depend on its required database. A passing migration test does not provide a real identity store, broker or durable outbox worker. Keep each boundary named in the deployment plan.

title: Spring Boot environment variables: bind the intended key, not a lookalike
summary: Spring Boot can bind an operating-system environment variable to a canonical configuration property after normalizing its name.
body:
Spring Boot can bind an operating-system environment variable to a canonical configuration property after normalizing its name.

Translate the key deliberately

For the relay setting relay.batch-size, replace the dot with an underscore, remove the dash, then use uppercase: RELAY_BATCHSIZE. RELAY_BATCH_SIZE looks natural, but it is a different spelling. Put the canonical property and its deployment spelling in the same change review. The typed settings bean should reject an unusable number after binding.

An environment variable usually outranks a packaged application file. It does not outrank every possible source: a command-line argument can still replace it. The earlier H2 collision shows why a programmatic default is especially weak. Record the final non-secret value and its source when diagnosing a rollout; do not print credential values.

Test the process that receives it

A test that inserts MapPropertySource into an Environment has not proved the operating system passed RELAY_BATCHSIZE to a launched process. A real boundary test must start a child process with that variable, inspect the bound value and stop it. RelaySettingsProcessTest now runs that child-process check and asserts batch 29 and timeout 750 milliseconds.

A typo may leave the packaged default active. If that default admits too many rows per tick, the worker budget changes without an obvious startup failure. For required deployment keys, validate both presence and range. Keep separate tests for CLI overrides, because the operator may intentionally supersede the environment.

Working sketch

RELAY_BATCHSIZE=29
# Canonical property: relay.batch-size
# Verify the value in a launched child process before release.

Verification boundary

RelaySettingsProcessTest.actualEnvironmentBindsTheCanonicalRelayKeys checks inherited environment values in a child JVM.

Costs and limits

The mapping is a documented configuration rule, not a checked deployment environment in this kit. Shells, container manifests and secret injection still need an end-to-end test.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not invent an extra underscore for a dash in a canonical key.
  • Do not treat a manual property source as a process-environment test.
  • Do not log a secret to explain property precedence.

title: Spring Boot relative config imports: resolve from the declaring file
summary: A relative config import is resolved from the file that declares it, which can differ from the process working directory.
body:
A relative config import is resolved from the file that declares it, which can differ from the process working directory.

Follow the declaring file

Suppose /etc/receipt/application.properties imports optional:relay/worker.properties. The relative path belongs beneath /etc/receipt, not beneath whichever directory the Java process started in. A nested import inside relay/worker.properties uses that nested file as its own base. A file: prefix selects a fixed path instead.

This matters during packaging. A local test might run from the repository root while a container starts from /app. If the import is optional, both starts can succeed with different values. The missing optional test proves only that fallback is allowed, not that the operator file was found.

Choose failure behavior by ownership

A required deployment file should fail startup when absent. The required-import fixture covers that narrow condition. A developer-only override can be optional, but its absence should be visible through a redacted startup diagnostic. Do not make a required credential optional to quiet a bad mount.

Move the same packaged artifact between two launch directories in a release test. Inspect the bound non-secret value after each start and confirm the expected file was loaded. RelaySettingsProcessTest now checks a relative import beneath a declaring file while the child starts in another directory. A container volume remains untested.

Working sketch

spring.config.import=optional:relay/worker.properties
# In /etc/receipt/application.properties, this resolves under /etc/receipt/relay/.

Verification boundary

RelaySettingsProcessTest.relativeImportUsesItsDeclaringFileOutsideTheWorkingDirectory checks a relative child-file import; RelaySettingsProcessTest now checks a second nested import.

Costs and limits

No mounted directory, container working-directory change or nested import is exercised by the Maven suite.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not resolve every relative import against the shell working directory.
  • Do not mistake optional startup for proof that a file loaded.
  • Do not put credential contents in a config-origin diagnostic.

title: Spring Boot graceful shutdown: finish accepted requests within a deadline
summary: Graceful shutdown gives accepted HTTP requests a bounded chance to finish while the server stops admitting new work.
body:
Graceful shutdown gives accepted HTTP requests a bounded chance to finish while the server stops admitting new work.

Budget the whole stop sequence

A receipt POST may be inside validation, a database transaction or an external call when termination begins. Set a shutdown-phase deadline that is longer than the expected in-flight request but shorter than the platform termination allowance. A 20-second Spring phase inside a 10-second container kill window cannot complete as intended.

The embedded server's graceful stop is part of application-context close. New requests may be rejected at the network layer, and persistent connections complicate what a client observes. A client that loses the response after a committed write needs an idempotency contract before retrying. Shutdown does not roll back every action already committed.

Prove the signal path

Run the packaged application as a child process, hold one bounded request open, send the platform's normal termination signal, and record whether the response finishes. Then try a new request. Repeat with the real ingress or proxy, because a direct loopback test misses connection draining in front of the process.

The current kit tests live health and authentication over loopback, not a shutdown signal. The readiness fixture shows a dependency outage; it does not prove termination behavior. The configured phase deadline is a policy until the deployed process test runs.

Working sketch

spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=20s
# Platform termination allowance must exceed this phase and its other stop work.

Verification boundary

No graceful-stop process test exists in the source kit. ReadinessHealthGroupHttpTest covers a different live HTTP boundary.

Costs and limits

The property is a release setting, not evidence that a proxy drains connections or that a committed POST response reaches the client.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not set the platform kill deadline shorter than the application stop budget.
  • Do not assume a lost response means a database transaction rolled back.
  • Do not infer server shutdown behavior from a direct context-close unit test.

title: Spring worker shutdown: release admission before a lease expires
summary: A scheduled worker must stop taking new records and account for in-flight claims when the application terminates.
body:
A scheduled worker must stop taking new records and account for in-flight claims when the application terminates.

Separate new work from owned work

The local poller uses a bounded batch and a lease token. On termination, cancel the next poll first. A record already claimed still needs one of two outcomes: finish delivery and acknowledge with its current token, or leave the claim to expire so another worker can retry. A stale worker must never acknowledge after another owner has renewed or replaced the lease.

Token-fenced acknowledgement and lease renewal are checked against H2. Those tests use direct calls and a logical clock. They do not demonstrate how the deployed scheduler receives a stop signal or how a broker publication is confirmed.

Do not promise exactly once

If the consumer commits and the worker dies before acknowledgement, the event returns after lease expiry. The lost-ack fixture checks this local replay; the consumer's event-ID reservation must make the second delivery safe. A shutdown hook cannot eliminate this interval.

Choose an in-flight deadline shorter than the lease or renew while work continues. Record backlog age, claims still active at stop and the number of expired leases after restart. The current source kit cancels a test scheduler cleanly, but no scheduler runs inside ReceiptApplication.

stop accepting new polls
finish or abandon each claimed event before the stop deadline
acknowledge only with the current lease token

  • Do not start a new batch after the stop decision.
  • Do not acknowledge with an expired lease token.
  • Do not claim graceful shutdown removes duplicate-delivery risk.

title: Spring readiness during termination: stop routing before stopping dependencies
summary: Readiness controls whether a process should receive new traffic; liveness answers whether restarting it may help.
body:
Readiness controls whether a process should receive new traffic; liveness answers whether restarting it may help.

Withdraw traffic in order

An instance about to stop should become unavailable to routing before its database pool or worker resources are torn down. Otherwise a load balancer can send a new receipt command into a half-closed application. Spring's availability state and Actuator health groups provide a place to expose that decision, but the platform's probe interval and ingress drain delay determine when traffic actually stops.

The existing HTTP test forces a test dependency DOWN and sees readiness return 503 while liveness remains 200. That does not test a termination event. External database trouble should not automatically turn liveness into failure; repeated restarts can increase the outage.

Measure the routing lag

A release test needs the real platform: withdraw readiness, timestamp the final routed request, then allow in-flight work to finish under the stop budget. Record errors across old and new instances while the rollout occurs. A loopback GET against one instance cannot show what the ingress did.

Keep the health response narrow. The security fixture exposes nested health paths without opening the API. Internal dependency details should remain protected, while the platform receives only the status it needs to route traffic.

Working sketch

management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
# Measure platform probe and routing lag during the actual rollout.

Verification boundary

ReadinessHealthGroupHttpTest checks local health groups and API access; no termination-routing test exists.

Costs and limits

No ingress, platform probe interval, SIGTERM path or multi-instance rollout is measured.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not tear down a required dependency before traffic is withdrawn.
  • Do not make every external outage a liveness failure.
  • Do not expose full health details on a public probe path.

title: Spring RestClient request factories: pin the transport you test
summary: RestClient is a synchronous HTTP client whose request factory determines the network transport used by each call.
body:
RestClient is a synchronous HTTP client whose request factory determines the network transport used by each call.

The classpath can change the transport

A client built without an explicit request factory may select a different implementation when HTTP libraries are added or removed. That can change connection-pool behavior, timeout support and error handling even when the call site stays the same. For a receipt-risk lookup, configure the transport deliberately and run the same library set in tests and the packaged artifact.

RestClient itself is reusable across threads. That does not make the upstream service fast, nor does it supply a safe retry policy. The timeout lesson treats the transport setting as part of a larger request deadline, and the retry lesson separates read calls from writes.

Keep response ownership visible

A synchronous request occupies a calling thread until it completes or fails. If a servlet handler calls the downstream service, enough simultaneous slow responses can exhaust its request workers. Bound the client call and the number of concurrent admissions; measure saturation with an actual slow local server, then with the real upstream failure mode.

RestClientBoundaryTest now runs an explicit SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory against a loopback HTTP server. The configuration below remains a design sketch; the checked test uses a concrete factory and a random local port. Do not extrapolate performance from reactive demand tests to this blocking client.

Working sketch

RestClient riskClient = RestClient.builder()
    .requestFactory(selectedRequestFactory)
    .baseUrl(riskServiceBaseUrl)
    .build();

Verification boundary

RestClientBoundaryTest.explicitFactoryReadsTheUpstreamResponse checks a selected SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory over loopback; the displayed generic factory variable is a design sketch.

Costs and limits

The selected factory, connection pool and timeout behavior require a packaged-artifact test with the chosen HTTP library.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume the same classpath always selects the same transport.
  • Do not call a blocking client non-blocking because the server also has WebFlux dependencies.
  • Do not treat a reusable client as proof of bounded upstream latency.

title: Spring HTTP client timeouts: bound the call inside the request deadline
summary: A downstream timeout is one part of the total deadline for a request that may also wait for a connection, execute SQL and serialize a response.
body:
A downstream timeout is one part of the total deadline for a request that may also wait for a connection, execute SQL and serialize a response.

Spend one budget

Suppose the public receipt endpoint allows 900ms. Spending 700ms on a risk lookup leaves only 200ms for connection acquisition, local validation, transaction commit and response delivery. Two retries of that 700ms call cannot fit. Write down a maximum elapsed time for the whole request, then allocate connect, response and retry budgets beneath it.

Different request factories expose different timeout controls. Select the actual factory first; test connect refusal, a server that accepts but never responds, and a slow body. A successful localhost response says nothing about these paths. The transport choice is part of the contract.

Keep transactions short

Do not hold a database transaction open while waiting on a slow third-party request unless the business rule truly requires it and the lock cost is understood. A client timeout after the remote server commits can still leave an uncertain result. The outbox boundary records local intent atomically, then performs external delivery separately.

The kit now checks an 80ms read timeout against a loopback server that accepts the request and stalls. The snippet remains a budget worksheet; it does not establish a 900ms end-to-end service deadline.

Working sketch

public request deadline: 900ms
connection acquisition + connect: 120ms
upstream response: 450ms
local transaction and response reserve: 330ms

Costs and limits

The budget is illustrative. Production values require measured latency distributions, the chosen transport and real upstream failure tests.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not add per-attempt timeouts that exceed the public request deadline.
  • Do not keep a database transaction open across an avoidable network wait.
  • Do not infer remote non-commit from a client-side timeout.

title: Spring HTTP retries: only replay a command with a defined identity
summary: A timeout after sending a remote write leaves its result uncertain, so retry safety depends on the upstream command contract.
body:
A timeout after sending a remote write leaves its result uncertain, so retry safety depends on the upstream command contract.

Differentiate reads from writes

A bounded GET may be repeated after a transient connection failure if the read has no side effect and the deadline permits another attempt. A POST that creates a payment or reserves inventory cannot be retried blindly. The remote side may have committed before the response was lost. Attach a stable command identifier only when the upstream accepts and enforces it.

The local POST fixture stores a response against a key but lives in one process. The tenant command fixture puts replay state in the same H2 transaction as the mutation. Neither proves the behavior of an external risk or payment service.

Treat retry as a state machine

Track original request, uncertain result, retry attempt, duplicate response and final reconciliation. Enforce a total deadline and an attempt cap. Retry only the failure classes that the upstream contract permits; a validation error should not enter a backoff loop. If the upstream cannot deduplicate, create a reconciliation path instead of claiming safe replay.

A consumer that receives an outbox event twice has the same identity problem. The event-ID ledger commits deduplication with its local mutation. The source kit now calls a local HTTP handler over loopback. It shows a write before timeout and a same-key replay against an in-memory deduplicating server; it still does not call a real downstream provider or prove durable deduplication.

Working sketch

POST /remote-reservations
Idempotency-Key: receipt-2048-tenant-east
# Reuse the same key only for the same normalized command.

Verification boundary

RestClientBoundaryTest.aTimedOutWriteMayHaveCommittedBeforeTheCallerRetries checks a sequential loopback replay; no external provider or distributed retry is tested.

Costs and limits

No production remote service, distributed failure injection or cross-system reconciliation test is present.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not generate a new key on every retry of the same command.
  • Do not replay an uncertain write against a server without a deduplication contract.
  • Do not retry validation failures as transient outages.

title: Spring release tests: distinguish context checks from process and platform checks
summary: A Spring context test proves bean behavior inside one process; it cannot by itself prove process signals, ingress routing or external transport.
body:
A Spring context test proves bean behavior inside one process; it cannot by itself prove process signals, ingress routing or external transport.

Write the test at the failing layer

For a configuration import, a non-web context is enough to check a missing local file. For RELAY_BATCHSIZE supplied by the OS, launch a child process with that environment. For graceful shutdown, terminate the packaged server with the normal signal while a request is active. For routing drain, place the same artifact behind the intended ingress and measure the last admitted request.

The general test guide separates unit, context and HTTP coverage. The current kit already has local HTTP health tests, config-import tests, staged H2 migration tests and outbox claim tests. These are evidence for their named local boundaries, not a production release rehearsal.

Capture state after failure

Do not stop at a response code. Read the receipt row, outbox row, replay key and migration history after each injected cut point. A lost response can follow a successful commit; an interrupted worker can leave a lease that another instance later claims. The relay trace lists those persisted states.

The source kit now also checks a loopback RestClient read timeout and uncertain write. The missing matrix still includes a target database, two application versions running together, a real broker, process kill between consumer commit and acknowledgement, and the actual proxy. An integration environment should run the exact packaged artifact and migration SQL. Keep each failure case bounded so a red test identifies the broken boundary.

Working sketch

1. Start the packaged old and new applications against a disposable target database.
2. Apply V2, send old and new writes, then stop one instance mid-request.
3. Inspect rows, outbox state and routed responses before applying V3.

Verification boundary

The existing Maven suite checks local contexts, H2 states and loopback HTTP; this multi-process matrix has not run.

Costs and limits

No target database, ingress, broker, process-kill setup or mixed-version deployment is included.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not label a context-close test a graceful platform shutdown test.
  • Do not assert only HTTP status while ignoring committed rows.
  • Do not apply a breaking migration before proving old-version retirement.

title: Spring Boot project: define the receipt service release boundary
summary: A receipt service release boundary joins configuration, database compatibility, HTTP drain and worker replay into one observable sequence.
body:
A receipt service release boundary joins configuration, database compatibility, HTTP drain and worker replay into one observable sequence.

Assemble a disposable rehearsal

Start from the last released schema on the intended database engine. Launch the old application version, apply the nullable expansion, then launch the new version. Keep both alive while reading and writing. Backfill from an authoritative tenant source; only after old writers leave should the NOT NULL phase run. The H2 migration project checks a sequential subset, not this live overlap.

Give the new version its actual environment variables and required imported files. Record redacted effective values. Route it behind the intended proxy, withdraw readiness and terminate it while one accepted request runs. The stop lesson names the response ambiguity that must be handled with a stable request identity.

Count recovery, not just success

Allow the relay to claim work, then kill it after the consumer commits but before acknowledgement. A replacement must wait for lease expiry, retry with the same event ID and avoid a second mutation. The local fake-transport fixture checks the state transition; this project requires a real broker and target database to establish the release behavior.

The source kit is still a teaching artifact. ReceiptApplication has fixture Basic credentials, in-memory receipts and no runtime Flyway or scheduler. Promote each dependency only after the corresponding integration test exists. Keep the full failure trace and timing measurements with the release candidate.

Working sketch

schema V1 -> nullable V2 -> old/new overlap -> verified backfill -> old retired -> V3
traffic admitted -> readiness withdrawn -> in-flight request resolved -> process stopped
claim -> publish -> consumer commit -> lost ack -> lease expiry -> deduplicated replay

Costs and limits

Target database, issuer, broker, proxy, deployment platform and mixed-version processes are not supplied by the kit.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not contract a column while an old writer still omits it.

title: Spring RestClient transport: run the factory you configured
summary: An explicit RestClient request factory makes the local network transport a deliberate part of a call contract.
body:
An explicit RestClient request factory makes the local network transport a deliberate part of a call contract.

The checked local call

RestClientBoundaryTest builds a client with SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory, a 300ms connect timeout and a one-second read timeout. A loopback server responds to GET /risk/receipt-2048 with approved. The test asserts the returned body, so it checks a real HTTP exchange through the selected factory rather than a stubbed RestClient response.

The same factory is reused in the stalled-response and uncertain-write checks. The architecture lesson explains why pinning the transport matters: classpath changes can alter an implicit selection. This test checks only the simple JDK-backed factory. It does not compare Apache, Jetty or JDK HttpClient implementations.

Scope the evidence

The server binds 127.0.0.1 on a random port and is stopped after each test. The response is tiny and local. It does not exercise TLS, DNS, connection pooling, proxies, response-body streaming or a remote upstream. The fixture shows how to wire a factory and inspect a real response; it does not establish production throughput.

Do not share a mutable setup object across concurrent requests without testing its thread behavior. Build the client once with the chosen factory and measure the packaged artifact under load. The deadline fixture supplies one more bounded transport check.

var factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
factory.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300));
factory.setReadTimeout(readTimeout);
return RestClient.builder()
    .requestFactory(factory)
    .baseUrl("http://127.0.0.1:" + upstream.getAddress().getPort())
    .build();

Costs and limits

One loopback exchange with a simple request factory is checked. No TLS, proxy, pool, remote latency or concurrent load is tested.

  • Do not call a loopback success test a production latency measurement.
  • Do not confuse a real local socket with a real external service.

title: Spring RestClient 503 response: count attempts before adding a retry
summary: A 503 response is a remote status, and the checked RestClient call makes one request before surfacing that failure.
body:
A 503 response is a remote status, and the checked RestClient call makes one request before surfacing that failure.

Count the local exchange

The loopback server increments a counter and returns 503 for the receipt-risk GET. RestClientBoundaryTest expects HttpServerErrorException from retrieve().body(String.class), then asserts that the server saw one request. This proves there is no implicit second attempt in this configured fixture. It does not prove every interceptor or future client configuration is retry-free.

A retry policy is an application decision. For an idempotent GET, another attempt may be allowed only if the total request deadline has room and the upstream contract permits it. The budget worksheet keeps the attempts inside the public request deadline.

Do not flatten all failures

A 503 means a server sent an HTTP response. The stalled-response case is different: it fails while waiting for bytes. Authentication errors, malformed responses and validation failures also need different policies. Retrying every exception can multiply load during an outage.

Record status class, attempt count and elapsed time using bounded labels. Do not put a receipt ID into a metric tag. The meter lesson explains the memory and backend cost of unbounded identities.
