title: Spring Resource Server JWT key rotation: overlap keys across token lifetime
summary: Publish a replacement verification key before issuing tokens with it, and retain the retiring key until old tokens and caches expire.
body:
Publish a replacement verification key before issuing tokens with it, and retain the retiring key until old tokens and caches expire.

A kid is a lookup hint

A signed JWT carries a key identifier that helps the decoder choose a public key from the issuer's JWK set. The signature still has to verify; a kid is not proof of trust. Spring Resource Server can obtain and refresh JWK data from the configured issuer. Keep the issuer and accepted algorithm policy deliberate, and retain issuer, audience and time validation alongside signature checks. If the application supplies its own JwtDecoder bean, configure validators explicitly and test a token from the wrong issuer; do not assume a builder method installed those validators.

Roll in two directions

First publish the new public key while still signing with the old private key. Wait for verifiers to fetch the new set, then begin signing new tokens. Keep the old public key until every old token can expire plus any relevant cache window. If the issuer drops it immediately, valid tokens can fail during rollout. If a compromised private key must be revoked immediately, accepting some old tokens is no longer safe; plan for an explicit user reauthentication event.

Test the outage path

Run a verifier against a controlled JWK endpoint: accept a token signed with the old key, add the new key, accept a new token, then remove the old key after its expiry window. Test an unknown kid while the endpoint is unavailable and inspect the chosen decoder's cache behavior. Do not assume every node refreshes at the same instant. Authentication failure mapping should distinguish bad credentials from a resource outage in logs without leaking key details to callers.

Implementation contract

spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=${JWT_ISSUER}

Cost and verification

JWK retrieval and cache misses add network and parse work. An overly short cache can overload the issuer; an overly long cache can delay planned rotation or emergency revocation. Measure the verifier's actual refresh behavior under load.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not remove the old public key as soon as new signing begins.
  • Do not accept a token merely because its kid matches a published key.
  • Do not assume a custom JwtDecoder carries issuer and audience validators unless you configured and tested them.

title: Spring password hash upgrade after a verified login
summary: Re-encode a legacy password only after a successful match, then replace the stored hash with a conditional update.
body:
Re-encode a legacy password only after a successful match, then replace the stored hash with a conditional update.

Verify before migration

A user account holds a stored password hash with an algorithm marker. DelegatingPasswordEncoder can choose the correct verifier for that marker and use a current encoder for new hashes. On a successful login, upgradeEncoding tells the application whether the stored encoding should be replaced. This is a write to credential state, not a reason to retain or log the raw password. Password storage basics] cover the format; this lesson covers rolling a live account set forward.

Protect concurrent changes

Two successful logins can both observe the old hash. A compare-and-set update keyed by user ID and old hash lets only one write the replacement; the other can safely continue because its credential check already succeeded. A password reset racing with login must win over a stale rehash, so do not update by user ID alone. If a legacy hash lacks an algorithm marker, define an explicit migration mapping rather than silently treating an unknown format as plaintext.

Measure the rollout

Count remaining legacy IDs and successful upgrades without emitting hashes or passwords. Exercise a successful legacy login, a failed password, a concurrent reset and a user whose hash is already current. Rehashing costs CPU and may increase login latency; cap login concurrency and tune the selected algorithm on deployment hardware. An upgrade-on-login path will never reach dormant accounts, so set a separate reset policy if the old format must be retired by a date.

Implementation contract

public void verifyAndUpgrade(String rawPassword, Account account) {
    String observedHash = account.passwordHash();
    if (!passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, observedHash)) {
        throw new BadCredentialsException("Invalid credentials");
    }
    if (passwordEncoder.upgradeEncoding(observedHash)) {
        String replacement = passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword);
        accounts.updateHashIfCurrent(
            account.id(), observedHash, replacement);
    }
}

Cost and verification

A password hash intentionally consumes CPU and memory. A login that upgrades pays one verification plus one new encoding, and the conditional database update adds a write. Rate limits and capacity planning matter during a broad migration.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not re-encode before confirming that the supplied password matches.
  • Do not overwrite a concurrent password reset with a stale login upgrade.
  • Do not log raw passwords, stored hashes or replacement hashes during migration.

title: Spring SecurityContext handoff to a bounded async executor
summary: Wrap a short-lived executor task with the submitting security context, then recheck authorization at the work boundary.
body:
Wrap a short-lived executor task with the submitting security context, then recheck authorization at the work boundary.

A thread does not inherit request identity safely

An HTTP handler submits receipt work to a thread pool. SecurityContextHolder is normally associated with the executing thread; an ordinary worker does not automatically receive the caller's Authentication. DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor wraps submissions so the task sees the captured context and clears it afterward. This is useful for short-lived request work. The transaction] is still separate, and trace context] has its own propagation path.

Keep authorization close to the effect

Capturing a security context does not make a queued task safe forever. The user may lose access before the task runs, or the token may expire. Pass a stable tenant and actor ID, re-evaluate any policy that must be current, and bound the queue so stale work does not pile up. For durable jobs, persist an explicit actor and command rather than a Java thread-local Authentication; durable delivery] has a different failure contract.

Test isolation between tasks

Submit two tasks from different authenticated callers and assert each sees only its own tenant. After each task, submit a task without authentication and assert it does not inherit the previous caller. Run rejection and cancellation cases through the bounded executor] to ensure no security context leaks when work never starts.

Implementation contract

@Bean("receiptSecurityExecutor")
AsyncTaskExecutor receiptSecurityExecutor(
        @Qualifier("receiptExecutor") AsyncTaskExecutor pool) {
    return new DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor(pool);
}

Cost and verification

Wrapping tasks adds context capture and restoration per submission. Queue delay is often the larger cost and can make a captured identity stale; keep capacity bounded and record the actor needed for audit.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume request SecurityContext automatically appears on an arbitrary pool thread.
  • Do not use a captured Authentication as the only authorization check for long-delayed work.
  • Do not confuse security-context propagation with transaction or trace-context propagation.

title: Spring Security CORS preflight: evaluate origin before authentication
summary: An OPTIONS preflight lacks ordinary credentials; configure a bounded CORS policy in the security chain before protected requests reach authorization.
body:
An OPTIONS preflight lacks ordinary credentials; configure a bounded CORS policy in the security chain before protected requests reach authorization.

Preflight is not the business request

A browser sends OPTIONS with an Origin and requested method before some cross-origin API calls. That preflight may have no session cookie or bearer token. Rejecting it for missing authentication prevents the browser from making a later valid POST. Spring Security can process CORS before authorization when a suitable configuration source is wired. The browser boundary] still does not replace server-side authentication.

Name allowed callers precisely

Accept one configured web origin, the required methods, and the exact headers used by the client. A wildcard origin with credentialed requests is a dangerous mismatch and may be rejected by browser rules. The example uses an environment-provided origin and does not permit credentials by default; a cookie-based application needs a separate, reviewed CSRF and cookie policy. Session CSRF] and bearer-token APIs should not be mixed casually.

Probe both requests

Send an OPTIONS request with a permitted Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method POST and Access-Control-Request-Headers Authorization. Assert the response permits the browser to continue without authenticating the preflight. Then send the actual POST without a valid token and require denial; a successful preflight grants no write access. Repeat with an unapproved origin and with multiple filter chains], since the selected chain controls the CORS policy.

Implementation contract

@Bean
UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource apiCors(
        @Value("${app.web-origin}") String webOrigin) {
    CorsConfiguration policy = new CorsConfiguration();
    policy.setAllowedOrigins(List.of(webOrigin));
    policy.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "OPTIONS"));
    policy.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type"));
    UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource source =
        new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
    source.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", policy);
    return source;
}

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain apiChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(rules ->
            rules.anyRequest().authenticated());
    return http.build();
}

Cost and verification

Preflight adds an extra browser round trip unless cached. A narrow policy costs little server CPU, but every new origin, method or header expands the cross-origin surface and should correspond to a real client requirement.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not require a bearer token on the OPTIONS preflight and then call the browser broken.
  • Do not treat a successful preflight as authorization for the actual request.
  • Do not apply a broad origin wildcard to a credentialed browser flow.

title: Spring Actuator management port: separate listener, explicit access rule
summary: Move operational endpoints to a separate listener when the network needs it, then secure that listener as a distinct entry point.
body:
Move operational endpoints to a separate listener when the network needs it, then secure that listener as a distinct entry point.

A port is a routing boundary

A receipt API serves customers on one listener while an operations network reaches a second. Setting management.server.port gives Actuator its own HTTP listener; management.server.address can bind that listener to an internal interface. Neither property authenticates callers. The network must restrict reachability, and the application must still decide which principals may inspect or change operations state. Security chains and health checks have separate jobs.

Review the security back-off

An application-defined SecurityFilterChain takes control of HTTP access rules. Do not assume Spring Boot will add a protective Actuator rule after that point. Give management requests an explicit matcher and authorization policy, and test it through the actual listener. A reverse proxy that forwards the management port onto the public host can undo the intended isolation. Prefer a narrow exposure list even behind a firewall.

Test the deployment path

Probe the application listener and management listener independently from an allowed operations host and a denied client host. Confirm an unauthenticated caller cannot reach a sensitive endpoint, even if the network rule is accidentally widened. Include a startup test for conflicting port and address settings, and verify service discovery does not advertise the management listener as a customer API. Readiness may need a deliberate exception for the platform probe.

Implementation contract

management.server.port=9471
management.server.address=${MANAGEMENT_BIND_ADDRESS:127.0.0.1}
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus

Cost and verification

A second listener consumes a small amount of memory and one port allocation. The main operational cost is maintaining two routing and access paths; every endpoint added to exposure expands what that path can reveal or change.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a separate port as authentication.
  • Do not define a custom SecurityFilterChain and assume Actuator access remains automatically protected.
  • Do not publish the management listener through the same public ingress without reviewing its route and credentials.

title: Spring Prometheus scrape endpoint: registry, exposure and label contract
summary: A metrics scrape needs the registry, an exposed endpoint and stable labels; the diagnostic metrics endpoint is a different interface.
body:
A metrics scrape needs the registry, an exposed endpoint and stable labels; the diagnostic metrics endpoint is a different interface.

Three pieces must agree

Adding Actuator alone does not make a Prometheus scrape. Include the Prometheus registry in the application, expose the prometheus endpoint over HTTP, and configure the collector to reach the instance through an allowed operations route. The scrape representation lives at the Actuator prometheus endpoint; metric-cardinality starts with what each meter labels. The Actuator metrics endpoint is useful for human inspection, but it is not the collector's scrape format.

Keep identity stable

A request counter tagged with customer ID creates one series per customer, which grows with traffic rather than with the small set of routes and outcomes. Tag by bounded route template, method and response class. Keep environment and service identity consistent across redeployments; do not put timestamps or pod IDs into a custom label when the collector already supplies target identity. A collector outage should not make the receipt API fail a request.

Check real samples

After deployment, fetch the scrape from the same network and credentials used by the collector. Assert that the receipt outcome counter is present after one success and one rejection, then inspect its distinct label combinations. A zero or missing series can mean no event occurred, a bean was not registered, the registry is absent, or the endpoint is not exposed. These are different faults and deserve different tests. Management routing determines where the collector connects.

Implementation contract

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,prometheus
management.metrics.tags.application=receipt-api

Cost and verification

Scraping walks and formats the registered meters on each interval. Series cost grows roughly with the product of distinct label values; keep that product bounded before choosing a short scrape interval.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not point a Prometheus collector at the diagnostic metrics endpoint.
  • Do not expose a scrape publicly just because it contains no customer response bodies.
  • Do not use receipt IDs, tenant IDs or request IDs as metric label values.

title: Spring health details: status for probes, diagnostics for operators
summary: Return a small status to routine probes while limiting component names and failure details to authorized operators.
body:
Return a small status to routine probes while limiting component names and failure details to authorized operators.

Health has two audiences

A scheduler wants a quick answer about whether a receipt instance can receive traffic. An operator may need to know which contributor is failing. A public probe response should not casually disclose database names, broker topology or exception text. The health show-details and show-components settings control how much information the endpoint returns; an authorization rule still determines who can call it. Readiness answers admission to traffic, while health design decides what each indicator measures.

Separate failure domains

Do not make liveness depend on a remote payment processor. A temporary remote outage is not proof that restarting the JVM will help, and a restart loop can amplify the outage. A readiness group may include a dependency if this instance truly cannot serve any request without it, but that decision can remove all instances at once during a shared failure. Put nonessential dependency signals in an operator-facing diagnostic group.

Verify both views

Call the probe path without credentials and inspect the exact response body. Then call the operator path with and without the permitted role. Assert that unauthorized output omits contributor details and that the authorized view identifies a forced failing contributor. Run the check behind the real proxy because path rewriting and separate management ports alter which rule sees the request. Keep indicator work bounded so a stalled dependency cannot occupy every probe worker.

Implementation contract

management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized
management.endpoint.health.show-components=when-authorized
management.endpoint.health.roles=OPS

Cost and verification

More health contributors add probe latency and may consume connection-pool slots. A deeply detailed response also increases the information exposed to anyone who can call that endpoint; cache or bound expensive diagnostics separately.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expose all health details to a public load balancer probe.
  • Do not add every remote dependency to liveness.
  • Do not assume a role setting replaces an explicit request authorization policy.

title: Spring cache after commit: keep rolled-back writes out of readers
summary: Publish cache invalidation after the database commits so a failed transaction cannot leave readers with an impossible state.
body:
Publish cache invalidation after the database commits so a failed transaction cannot leave readers with an impossible state.

The database decides first

A receipt update can pass validation, write a row and still roll back when a later constraint fails. Updating a shared cache inside that transaction lets another request observe a value the database never committed. An after-commit event moves invalidation to the success side of the boundary. Eviction then makes the next read load durable state. The event handler below is short and deliberately does not contact another service.

Know the remaining gap

After-commit work runs in the same process and can be lost if the process stops between commit and eviction. Give entries a bounded TTL, and use a durable change record when strict cross-node invalidation is required. A transaction-aware cache decorator can defer ordinary put, evict and clear operations until commit, but immediate atomic operations such as putIfAbsent have different timing. Read the behavior of the chosen CacheManager rather than assuming every cache action is deferred.

Test two timelines

First commit a receipt edit and verify that a subsequent reader sees the new stored value. Then force a rollback after the edit and verify no invalidation event ran. Exercise a node restart just after commit: TTL should eventually repair the stale entry, while a durable relay is needed for a tighter freshness guarantee. Transaction events and an outbox relay define those different delivery promises.

Implementation contract

@Component
final class ReceiptCacheInvalidator {
    private final CacheManager cacheManager;

    ReceiptCacheInvalidator(CacheManager cacheManager) {
        this.cacheManager = cacheManager;
    }

    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    void on(ReceiptChanged changed) {
        Cache receiptCache = cacheManager.getCache("receipt-view-v3");
        if (receiptCache != null) receiptCache.evict(changed.cacheKey());
    }
}

Cost and verification

An invalidation adds one cache write after each committed edit and the next read pays a cache miss. A durable relay adds storage and retry work, but closes the process-crash gap that an in-memory event cannot close.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not populate shared cache state from a transaction that may roll back.
  • Do not assume an after-commit in-memory handler is durable across process failure.
  • Do not assume every atomic cache operation waits until commit.

title: Spring null-result caching: decide whether a miss should survive
summary: A missing record can be deliberately uncached or cached briefly; either choice changes load and freshness after creation.
body:
A missing record can be deliberately uncached or cached briefly; either choice changes load and freshness after creation.

A miss is an outcome

A receipt may be absent because it was never created, because replication has not caught up, or because the caller cannot see it. These cases should not automatically share one cache key or retention policy. With @Cacheable, an unless expression can veto storage after the method returns; the example does not cache null. Tenant-aware keys prevent one tenant's miss from masking another tenant's receipt. Do not encode authorization failure as a cached absence.

Choose the load tradeoff

Never caching misses preserves immediate visibility when a receipt is created, but repeated requests for unknown IDs all reach the database. A short negative cache can protect the database under repeated bad lookups, but a newly created record remains invisible until invalidation or expiry. If the result type is Optional, Spring evaluates #result against its contained value, so an empty Optional is still a null business result for this expression. Check what the selected provider stores when nulls are allowed.

Exercise creation after absence

Query an absent receipt, create it, and query again through the same API. With a no-null policy, the second read should reach storage and return it. For negative caching, add an explicit create-time invalidation and assert its behavior across nodes and rollback. Count misses by bounded route and outcome, never by receipt ID. Commit timing matters for that invalidation, and expiry limits the damage when a signal is lost.

Implementation contract

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "receipt-view-v3",
           key = "#p0 + ':' + #p1",
           unless = "#result == null")
public ReceiptView findVisibleReceipt(String tenantId, String receiptId) {
    return receipts.findVisible(tenantId, receiptId).orElse(null);
}

Cost and verification

Skipping null storage increases repeated database work for missing IDs. Negative caching reduces that work but spends capacity on misses and adds a freshness window that must be accepted by the product contract.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not share a missing-result key across tenants or authorization scopes.
  • Do not cache an empty result indefinitely when the record may be created later.
  • Do not use a null cache entry to hide an authorization failure.

title: Spring Redis cache serialization: roll payload formats without mixed readers
summary: Version the cache namespace before a payload or serializer change so old values are never decoded under a new contract.
body:
Version the cache namespace before a payload or serializer change so old values are never decoded under a new contract.

Cache entries have a wire format

A receipt view stored in Redis is bytes, not a Java object shared in memory. A serializer change, renamed field or new application version can make an existing entry unreadable. Treat the cache name and prefix as a format boundary: write the new view under receipt-view-v4 while old nodes continue using receipt-view-v3. Key schemas cover tenant and identifier separation; the version covers payload interpretation.

Roll forward in stages

Deploy code that can read its new namespace and refill it from the database. Keep the old namespace until old nodes leave traffic, then let its TTL retire entries. Do not mass-delete a shared Redis instance just to clear one application cache. Pin the serializer in configuration, test real encoded bytes from the previous release, and reject permissive polymorphic decoding of untrusted values. If two versions must share keys, use a deliberately backward-compatible envelope and a migration test instead of hope.

Measure the cold interval

A new namespace produces a temporary cache-miss wave. Stage rollout capacity, rate-limit expensive rebuilds and record miss ratio by bounded cache name. Test an old payload, a new payload, a corrupted value and an entry written by a node mid-rollout. A corrupt cache entry should not silently become a wrong receipt; classify and evict it or fail the request according to the data contract. Commit-safe invalidation remains necessary after writes.

Implementation contract

spring.cache.cache-names=receipt-view-v4
spring.cache.redis.time-to-live=47m
spring.cache.redis.use-key-prefix=true
spring.cache.redis.key-prefix=receipt-api:

Cost and verification

A version change temporarily duplicates old and new entries and increases database reads while the new cache warms. TTL bounds the old storage footprint; coordinated deployment and targeted metrics bound the cold-cache load.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not change a serializer while leaving old and new nodes on the same undecorated cache keys.
  • Do not clear an entire shared Redis database to retire one payload format.
  • Do not permit broad untrusted type deserialization merely to read legacy entries.

title: Spring tracing and logs: preserve request identity across outbound calls
summary: Correlate logs with trace and span IDs while using instrumented client builders for outbound propagation.
body:
Correlate logs with trace and span IDs while using instrumented client builders for outbound propagation.

Correlation is a path, not a tag dump

A receipt request may pass through an API, a pricing service and a worker. With tracing enabled, the logging context can carry trace and span identifiers so an operator can join a log line to the request path. Those identifiers are not a substitute for a stable business receipt ID in an audit record, and the receipt ID should not become a high-cardinality metric label. Metrics labels and async trace handoff require their own controls.

Use managed builders

Spring Boot customizes its injected RestClient.Builder and WebClient.Builder for observation and trace propagation when the required instrumentation is present. Constructing a raw client outside that path may omit propagation, even if incoming requests have trace IDs. The example accepts the managed builder and a configured service base address. Avoid printing authorization headers or customer payloads to compensate for missing trace context; repair the client path instead.

Check a complete hop

Send one request with a test trace context, capture logs on both services and verify the same trace ID appears on the inbound and outbound sides while span IDs differ where work is nested. Repeat through a queued task: a thread-local context may be absent unless the executor captures it. Sampling means an unsampled request can still have correlation identifiers but no stored trace; logs must remain useful without assuming every trace is retained. Client builder wiring is the companion implementation lesson.

Implementation contract

@Bean
RestClient receiptPartnerClient(
        RestClient.Builder managedBuilder,
        @Value("${receipt.partner-base}") String partnerBase) {
    return managedBuilder.baseUrl(partnerBase).build();
}

Cost and verification

Trace propagation adds small headers and context work per call; collecting and retaining spans costs more. Sample by an explicit policy, and keep log fields bounded so correlation does not become an uncontrolled data-export path.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not construct a raw HTTP client and assume it received Boot's trace customization.
  • Do not use customer IDs, tokens or payloads as trace tags or log correlation fields.
  • Do not treat a missing stored span as proof that the request never happened.

title: Spring Actuator loggers endpoint: temporary diagnosis with guarded write access
summary: Runtime log-level changes can help diagnose a narrow fault, but the endpoint is a privileged write interface.
body:
Runtime log-level changes can help diagnose a narrow fault, but the endpoint is a privileged write interface.

Viewing and changing are different powers

The loggers endpoint reports configured and effective levels and can accept a write for a named logger. That write can suddenly emit large volumes of sensitive application detail. Expose the endpoint only through the operations route, require a role authorized to change configuration, and record who made the change outside the application log level being modified. A management listener narrows network reach but does not supply authorization.

Scope the intervention

Raise logging for the smallest package involved in a receipt failure, set a short investigation window, and restore the previous level. Changing the root logger to DEBUG under production load can bury the signal, exhaust log transport and include request headers if existing code logs them. A runtime level change need not survive restart; use reviewed configuration for a permanent setting. Prefer trace correlation to broad debug output when following one request.

Verify denial and rollback

From an unprivileged account, test both read and write requests to the endpoint. From the operations role, change one named logger, confirm its effective level, then restore the prior configured level and confirm normal volume returns. Exercise a restart and check that the intended baseline wins. Keep an operational record of the affected service, instance, logger, actor and expiration time without logging credentials or payloads.

Implementation contract

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,loggers
logging.level.com.aitrove.receipts=INFO

Cost and verification

The endpoint itself is cheap when idle. A broad DEBUG setting can multiply log bytes, CPU formatting work and downstream storage charges; bound the logger and duration before enabling it.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not grant runtime logger writes to every authenticated user.
  • Do not change the root logger for a narrow production issue.
  • Do not assume a runtime change is a permanent configuration update.

title: Spring MVC async executor: bound Callable work before requests pile up
summary: Returning Callable frees the servlet request thread, but the work still needs a bounded executor and a timeout budget.
body:
Returning Callable frees the servlet request thread, but the work still needs a bounded executor and a timeout budget.

Async does not erase work

A receipt export handler can return Callable while Spring releases the initial servlet thread. The callable then runs on an AsyncTaskExecutor, and the response remains open until a second dispatch completes it. If submissions outrun workers, an unbounded queue turns latency into memory pressure. Configure the executor used by Spring MVC rather than assuming the default has production capacity. Async boundaries explain why a thread switch also changes context and transaction behavior.

Budget the whole request

Set an MVC async timeout shorter than the upstream proxy deadline, and give every database or outbound call its own tighter deadline. A response timeout does not automatically stop a blocking connector; it can continue holding a worker after the client has gone. Use a bounded queue and define rejection behavior that produces a clear overload response. Executor rejection should be tested at capacity, not only when the system is idle.

Test saturation

Hold all worker threads with controlled tasks, fill the queue, and submit another receipt request. Verify the request fails within its deadline rather than waiting indefinitely. Release the tasks and confirm the executor recovers. Run the same case through the load balancer to check that its timeout is later than the application timeout. A successful unit test of the callable body says nothing about servlet redispatch or queueing.

Implementation contract

@Configuration
class ReceiptMvcAsyncConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    private final AsyncTaskExecutor receiptExecutor;

    ReceiptMvcAsyncConfig(
            @Qualifier("receiptExecutor") AsyncTaskExecutor receiptExecutor) {
        this.receiptExecutor = receiptExecutor;
    }

    @Override
    public void configureAsyncSupport(AsyncSupportConfigurer support) {
        support.setTaskExecutor(receiptExecutor);
        support.setDefaultTimeout(4700L);
    }
}

Cost and verification

Each active callable occupies a worker and its open response holds connection state. Queue capacity bounds memory but creates explicit rejections; sizing should follow measured work duration and peak concurrent requests.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not confuse releasing the servlet thread with finishing the request.
  • Do not leave blocking callable work on an unbounded default executor.
  • Do not assume a servlet timeout cancels a database or remote call.

title: Spring MVC streaming response: stop work when the client disconnects
summary: A streaming response shifts output to an executor; close its cursor and end production when a write fails.
body:
A streaming response shifts output to an executor; close its cursor and end production when a write fails.

Stream from a bounded source

A receipt CSV export may contain enough rows that building one byte array would consume excessive heap. StreamingResponseBody writes chunks directly to the response, but it does not give the export unlimited time or free threads. Use the configured MVC async executor and a database cursor or paged reader with an explicit resource lifetime. Executor capacity sets the concurrency ceiling; upload limits protect the opposite direction.

Treat write failure as cancellation

A browser that closes its download may cause a write or flush to throw IOException. Stop reading further rows and let try-with-resources close the cursor. Do not catch the exception and keep generating receipts; doing so burns database work for a socket that no longer exists. If the export is a durable business job rather than an interactive download, persist its progress and let the client fetch a completed artifact instead of holding one HTTP connection open.

Prove cleanup under a broken connection

Start an export of 47 rows, close the client after the first chunk, and assert the cursor closes promptly while later rows are not fetched. Repeat with a slow reader and a server shutdown. Once headers or bytes have been written, an error handler often cannot replace the response with a clean JSON problem body; record the failure server-side without leaking receipt contents. Shutdown draining needs an explicit deadline for these long responses.

Implementation contract

@GetMapping(value = "/receipts/export", produces = "text/csv")
StreamingResponseBody exportReceipts() {
    return output -> {
        try (ReceiptCursor cursor = receipts.openExportCursor()) {
            while (cursor.hasNext()) {
                output.write(cursor.nextCsvRow());
            }
            output.flush();
        }
    };
}

Cost and verification

Streaming reduces peak heap from the full export size to a row and output buffer, but every active download still holds a worker, cursor and connection until completion or failure.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not retain an open database cursor after a client disconnect.
  • Do not catch IOException and continue generating the rest of the export.
  • Do not promise a structured error body after response bytes have already been sent.

title: Spring WebFlux codec memory budget: distinguish aggregation from streaming
summary: Set an in-memory decode ceiling for WebClient payloads and stream large responses instead of merely lifting the limit.
body:
Set an in-memory decode ceiling for WebClient payloads and stream large responses instead of merely lifting the limit.

Aggregation has a ceiling

A WebClient call that decodes one JSON receipt document may buffer bytes before producing an object. The codec maxInMemorySize setting places a cap on that aggregation. When a partner sends a much larger body, raising the cap to match its biggest possible response multiplies memory exposure by concurrent requests. Decide whether that body is legitimate; if so, change the processing shape to a stream or file transfer rather than silently accepting an unbounded object. Response ownership still matters when handling status branches.

Size the limit from a contract

Measure a normal receipt response, allow bounded headroom and configure the client that calls that partner. The example caps in-memory decoding at 384 KiB for one client. A separate client for genuinely large exports may use a different strategy. This setting does not cap every byte travelling through the network and does not replace a proxy request-size limit. A stream can still accumulate unbounded data if downstream code calls collectList or joins all buffers.

Probe failure and recovery

Return a payload just below the limit, one above it, and a chunked response that never ends. Verify a predictable failure for the oversized aggregate, a response deadline for the endless stream, and no retained connection after cancellation. Repeated oversize failures should not exhaust the connection pool. Reactive demand governs downstream consumption, while cancellation governs stopped work.

Implementation contract

@Bean
WebClient receiptPartnerClient(WebClient.Builder managedBuilder) {
    return managedBuilder
        .codecs(codecs -> codecs.defaultCodecs()
            .maxInMemorySize(384 * 1024))
        .build();
}

Cost and verification

The limit bounds memory per aggregated response, not the number of concurrent responses. At 384 KiB each, 47 simultaneous decodes can still reserve substantial heap before object allocation and application processing.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not solve every DataBufferLimitException by setting a very large global cap.
  • Do not collect an entire stream into a list and call it streaming.
  • Do not treat codec memory limits as request or response deadlines.

title: Spring WebClient status-specific decoding: consume one branch and close the rest
summary: Use exchangeToMono when success, absence and failure have different body contracts, and keep decoding inside the exchange callback.
body:
Use exchangeToMono when success, absence and failure have different body contracts, and keep decoding inside the exchange callback.

The status chooses the body type

A partner returns a receipt quote on success, an empty body for not-found and a problem document for other failures. retrieve is concise for a uniform success body, but exchangeToMono lets the client choose decoding based on status. The response body must be consumed or released within that exchange lifecycle; returning ClientResponse for later decoding breaks ownership. Response ownership covers the connection consequences of this boundary.

Preserve distinct business outcomes

A 404 for an optional quote can become Mono.empty, while a 401 or 503 must stay a failure. Do not turn every non-2xx into empty; that masks revoked credentials and partner outages as missing business data. The example delegates other failures to createError so the error body is handled by the client API. Add a separate bounded decoder when the partner's problem response needs structured fields, and keep codec memory limits in force for that error body too.

Test the release path

Feed a success body, an empty 404 and a failing response with a body through a test server. Reuse the connection after each path, and cancel a request while it is decoding to expose leaks. A downstream retry should be limited to operations that are safe to replay; decoding an error does not make a POST idempotent. Uncertain commit explains why a transport failure after a write needs a separate business key.

Implementation contract

Mono<ReceiptQuote> quote(String receiptId) {
    return partnerClient.get()
        .uri("/quotes/{receiptId}", receiptId)
        .exchangeToMono(response -> {
            if (response.statusCode().is2xxSuccessful()) {
                return response.bodyToMono(ReceiptQuote.class);
            }
            if (response.statusCode().value() == 404) {
                return Mono.empty();
            }
            return response.createError();
        });
}

Cost and verification

Status inspection is constant work. Body decoding and error buffering dominate memory and latency; a missing-result branch saves object allocation, but retries or repeated misses can still produce high request volume.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not return ClientResponse for decoding after exchangeToMono completes.
  • Do not map authentication and service failures to the same empty result as a true 404.
  • Do not retry a write merely because its response body could not be decoded.

title: Spring singleton state: one bean does not mean one request at a time
summary: A singleton instance is shared by concurrent callers; keep request-specific values outside its fields and publish shared state safely.
body:
A singleton instance is shared by concurrent callers; keep request-specific values outside its fields and publish shared state safely.

Scope is an identity rule

Spring's default singleton scope creates one bean instance per container definition. It does not serialize calls to that instance. A receipt pricer used by many HTTP requests must not keep the current tenant or a mutable calculation buffer in instance fields, because another thread can overwrite them mid-request. Constructor-injected collaborators can remain shared when they are safe for concurrent use. Bean scope controls instance creation; it is not a locking strategy.

Make the state contract explicit

The example copies a startup rate table into an immutable map and keeps currency and amount as method arguments. If rates must change while the process runs, publish an immutable snapshot through an AtomicReference or use a store with an explicit update protocol. A ConcurrentHashMap prevents structural corruption but does not make a read-modify-write business operation atomic. Per-request information can live in a request-scoped object when an HTTP request truly owns its lifetime; request proxies have their own boundary.

Test interleaving, not just output

Launch two requests for different tenants with a barrier between rate lookup and calculation. Verify neither can observe the other's tenant or amount. Run the test repeatedly under a thread pool; a single sequential test cannot expose a field race. For a hot rate reload, test that each calculation reads one complete snapshot rather than a mixture of old and new entries. Async work may outlive the HTTP request, so pass explicit values rather than reaching into request state later.

Implementation contract

@Service
final class ReceiptPricing {
    private final Map<String, BigDecimal> rates;

    ReceiptPricing(ReceiptRateProperties settings) {
        this.rates = Map.copyOf(settings.rates());
    }

    BigDecimal total(String currency, BigDecimal subtotal) {
        BigDecimal rate = Objects.requireNonNull(rates.get(currency));
        return subtotal.multiply(rate).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
    }
}

Cost and verification

An immutable snapshot adds one copy at startup and allows lock-free reads afterward. A mutable shared table may save a copy but requires a coherent update protocol and contention control under concurrent requests.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not store the current tenant, request ID or intermediate total in singleton fields.
  • Do not assume ConcurrentHashMap makes a multi-step business update atomic.
  • Do not inject a prototype once into a singleton and expect a new collaborator for every call.

title: Spring generic autowiring: preserve type arguments at the injection point
summary: Generic type arguments can distinguish candidate beans without a string qualifier when the bean signatures retain that type information.
body:
Generic type arguments can distinguish candidate beans without a string qualifier when the bean signatures retain that type information.

A raw interface is ambiguous

Two receipt encoders implement the same Encoder interface but produce different output models. Asking for Encoder without its type argument leaves the container with multiple candidates. Asking for Encoder<PdfReceipt> can select the PDF bean when its declared type retains the parameter. This is a compile-time type relationship used by container metadata, not a runtime check that the returned PDF bytes are valid. Explicit qualifiers still help when two beans share the same generic type.

Keep factory signatures informative

A factory method that declares Object, a raw Encoder, or an overly broad base type can hide the parameter Spring needs to select a candidate. Declare Encoder<PdfReceipt> and Encoder<CsvReceipt> on the bean methods even if the implementations are concrete classes. Generic selection also applies to lists: List<Encoder<PdfReceipt>> should contain only matching candidates. Do not make a new marker interface for every representation when the generic contract already expresses the difference.

Prove the chosen bean

Refresh a minimal context containing both encoders and inject a coordinator that requires Encoder<PdfReceipt>. Assert the selected implementation and output type. Add a second PDF encoder and require the context to report ambiguity until a qualifier or primary policy resolves it. This catches accidental signature erasure during a refactor. Primary selection is a separate fallback and may hide the wrong candidate if used casually.

Implementation contract

@Bean
Encoder<PdfReceipt> signedPdfEncoder(SigningKey key) {
    return new SignedPdfReceiptEncoder(key);
}

@Bean
Encoder<CsvReceipt> csvReceiptEncoder() {
    return new CsvReceiptEncoder();
}

final class ReceiptDownloadService {
    ReceiptDownloadService(Encoder<PdfReceipt> pdfEncoder) {
        this.pdfEncoder = pdfEncoder;
    }
    private final Encoder<PdfReceipt> pdfEncoder;
}

Cost and verification

Generic matching is resolved at wiring time, so request-path overhead is effectively unchanged. The cost is maintaining accurate method signatures and context tests as new implementations are registered.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not erase generic type arguments from @Bean return types.
  • Do not assume generics distinguish two candidates with the same parameterized type.
  • Do not use @Primary to conceal an unintended duplicate registration.

title: Spring @Lookup: obtain a fresh prototype from a singleton method
summary: Method injection lets a container-created singleton request a new prototype on each call, with subclassing limits that must be tested.
body:
Method injection lets a container-created singleton request a new prototype on each call, with subclassing limits that must be tested.

The lifetime mismatch is real

A singleton receipt renderer needs an isolated mutable render session for each document. Direct constructor injection of a prototype creates one session when the singleton starts, then reuses it. An @Lookup method asks the container to supply the session when rendering begins. ObjectProvider is often simpler because the dependency is explicit; use method injection when the collaborator must remain hidden behind a protected factory method.

Container creation is required

Spring implements lookup method injection by overriding a method on a generated subclass. The host class and lookup method cannot be final. A class built by an ordinary @Bean factory method does not get this lookup override because the container did not construct the instance in the required way. Register the host as a scanned component and mark the session prototype. A lookup of a singleton target still returns the same target each time; the annotation does not change the target scope.

Test identity and cleanup

Render two receipts and assert distinct session identities. Run parallel renders and check that temporary row buffers never cross documents. The container creates prototype instances, but it does not automatically run their destruction callbacks at the end of your method; explicitly close a session that owns a file or socket. Cleanup is a separate contract, and a unit test that directly calls an abstract lookup method cannot prove the runtime subclass was installed.

Implementation contract

@Component
abstract class ReceiptRenderCoordinator {
    byte[] render(ReceiptDocument document) {
        return newSession().render(document);
    }

    @Lookup
    protected abstract ReceiptRenderSession newSession();
}

@Component
@Scope(ConfigurableBeanFactory.SCOPE_PROTOTYPE)
class ReceiptRenderSession {
    private final ByteArrayOutputStream buffer = new ByteArrayOutputStream();

    byte[] render(ReceiptDocument document) {
        document.writePdfTo(buffer);
        return buffer.toByteArray();
    }
}

Cost and verification

Each call performs a container lookup and allocates a session. That is reasonable for document rendering, but a hot inner loop should not create a prototype per row or rely on automatic cleanup of external resources.

  • Do not mark the host class or lookup method final.
  • Do not instantiate the host through a normal @Bean factory method and expect lookup overriding.
  • Do not assume a prototype's destroy callback runs when the render method returns.

title: Spring synchronous event listener failure: publication can fail the caller
summary: Default application event delivery runs listeners in the publisher's thread, so listener latency and exceptions become part of the caller's result.
body:
Default application event delivery runs listeners in the publisher's thread, so listener latency and exceptions become part of the caller's result.

Publication is usually a method call

A receipt service publishes ReceiptAccepted while saving a row. With the default multicaster, listeners run synchronously on that thread. A listener that throws can stop publication and propagate its exception to the service; if the service is still inside a transaction, that may roll back the save. An event name does not make the work asynchronous or durable. Application events are local in-process communication, and transaction phase listeners move selected work to a different commit point.

Define the failure owner

A required invariant, such as updating a same-database receipt index, can legitimately fail the command. A best-effort notification should not decide whether the receipt is accepted. Move the latter after commit and give it a retryable durable channel if losing it matters. Configuring a multicaster ErrorHandler to swallow every listener failure can make a broken required listener invisible; assign failure handling per use case rather than globally masking exceptions.

Exercise rollback and ordering

Register a listener that records a call, then one that throws. Publish inside a transaction and assert the command's database state matches the intended failure contract. Do not depend on an incidental listener iteration order; if order matters, declare it and test it, or call a service directly when the steps form one business operation. Measure listener duration because synchronous listeners extend request latency and hold the publisher's resources.

Implementation contract

@Component
final class ReceiptIndexListener {
    private final ReceiptIndex receiptIndex;

    ReceiptIndexListener(ReceiptIndex receiptIndex) {
        this.receiptIndex = receiptIndex;
    }

    @EventListener
    void on(ReceiptAccepted accepted) {
        receiptIndex.record(accepted.receiptId());
    }
}

Cost and verification

Each synchronous listener adds its execution time to publishEvent and may hold the caller's transaction open. A slow remote call inside a listener can extend lock time and cause retries elsewhere.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume @EventListener makes delivery asynchronous or durable.
  • Do not swallow every listener error when some listeners enforce required state.
  • Do not call a remote service inside a transaction-scoped listener without a clear failure budget.

title: Spring async event listener: handle detached failures and queue pressure
summary: An @Async event listener releases the publisher quickly, but its exception, executor capacity and transaction context need separate handling.
body:
An @Async event listener releases the publisher quickly, but its exception, executor capacity and transaction context need separate handling.

The caller no longer owns completion

An @Async @EventListener runs on an executor when async support is enabled and the listener is invoked through the Spring-managed path. A void listener's exception does not propagate to the event publisher. Configure error reporting for that executor path, and treat a rejected submission as a distinct overload condition. Synchronous listeners have the opposite failure relationship; choose deliberately rather than adding @Async to silence a slow request.

Pass stable data

The worker thread does not inherit the publisher's transaction. Passing a managed entity that expects an open persistence context can fail or read unexpected state. Publish IDs and immutable values, then load the required state in the worker's own transaction if needed. Even after-commit delivery remains in-memory; a crash can erase accepted work. For a receipt that must reach another system, durable delivery and an outbox are the relevant boundary.

Prove error visibility

Force the listener's target to throw and assert an observable failure record or error-handler call while the publisher's result remains as designed. Fill the executor queue and test whether the event is rejected, blocked or sent to another path. Use a fixed clock and controlled executor in tests so completion timing is deterministic. A log line from a worker is insufficient proof of delivery to a remote recipient.

Implementation contract

@Component
final class ReceiptSearchListener {
    private final ReceiptSearchIndex searchIndex;

    ReceiptSearchListener(ReceiptSearchIndex searchIndex) {
        this.searchIndex = searchIndex;
    }

    @Async("receiptEventExecutor")
    @EventListener
    void on(ReceiptCommitted committed) {
        searchIndex.refresh(committed.receiptId());
    }
}

Cost and verification

The publisher saves listener latency, but each pending event consumes queue space and may become stale. A bounded executor makes overload explicit; an outbox adds storage and replay cost when completion must survive process failure.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect a void async listener exception to reach publishEvent.
  • Do not pass a lazy JPA entity to a detached worker thread.
  • Do not call an in-memory async listener a durable integration channel.

title: Spring AOP final methods: advice requires an interceptable call
summary: Class-based proxies cannot override final or private methods, and self-calls bypass proxy advice even when the method is open.
body:
Class-based proxies cannot override final or private methods, and self-calls bypass proxy advice even when the method is open.

The proxy is the boundary

A receipt reservation annotated @Transactional receives advice when another bean calls it through the Spring proxy. A direct call on this from inside the same object does not cross the proxy. With class-based proxying, a final class cannot be subclassed and a final or private method cannot be overridden for advice. Interface-based proxies have different method visibility, but they do not make private internal calls interceptable. Self-invocation and method security share this shape.

Put the boundary on a service API

Make the advised operation a public, non-final method on a bean injected into its caller. Keep helpers private if they do not require independent advice. If the operation needs a second transaction, move it to a separate service rather than trying to manipulate proxy internals. The example gives an order service a distinct ledger collaborator; the caller crosses the proxy at reserve, so transaction advice can run. A comment on a private helper would not change execution.

Test the behavior, not the annotation

Call the service through the application context, force a repository failure and assert the reservation rolls back. Then test a direct internal call only if the design still has one, so the test makes the difference visible. A unit test that constructs ReceiptLedger with new bypasses Spring advice and cannot prove transaction or security semantics. Proxy type may change with configuration, so prefer behavioral checks over assertions on generated class names.

Implementation contract

@Service
class ReceiptLedger {
    private final ReservationRepository reservations;

    ReceiptLedger(ReservationRepository reservations) {
        this.reservations = reservations;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void reserve(ReceiptCommand command) {
        reservations.insert(command.receiptId(), command.amount());
    }
}

@Service
class ReceiptOrderService {
    ReceiptOrderService(ReceiptLedger ledger) { this.ledger = ledger; }
    private final ReceiptLedger ledger;
    void accept(ReceiptCommand command) { ledger.reserve(command); }
}

Cost and verification

A proxy adds small dispatch overhead compared with database work. The real cost of a misplaced boundary is silent loss of transaction, cache, async or authorization behavior; an integration test is cheaper than recovering corrupted state.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not put @Transactional on a private or final method and expect class-based advice.
  • Do not call an advised method through this and expect the proxy to intercept it.
  • Do not prove AOP behavior with only a new-constructed unit object.

title: Spring Boot ConditionalOnMissingBean: a default that yields to application code
summary: An auto-configuration can provide a fallback bean while letting an application supply its own implementation by type.
body:
An auto-configuration can provide a fallback bean while letting an application supply its own implementation by type.

The condition sees definitions so far

A shared receipt starter supplies a default ReceiptGateway, but one application needs a signed gateway. @ConditionalOnMissingBean can skip the default when a compatible application bean is already registered. Put this condition in auto-configuration, which is processed after user bean definitions, rather than scattering it among ordinary application configurations whose ordering may surprise you. Auto-configuration selects a default; @Primary merely chooses among beans that both exist.

Publish the integration contract

The auto-configuration class must be registered through the starter's auto-configuration imports resource. Declare a concrete return type that allows the condition to see the bean's intended API. A broad Object return type or a factory whose type cannot be predicted can produce an unexpected default. Test the starter in isolation and with a user ReceiptGateway implementation; the first case must create exactly one gateway, the second must leave the user's bean in place.

Do not hide configuration failure

A missing required signing key is not a reason to silently instantiate an insecure fallback. Conditional creation answers whether a bean is already supplied; property validation answers whether the chosen gateway can start safely. Startup validation should fail for invalid settings. Inspect the condition outcome when a bean is unexpectedly present, and keep any override behavior explicit in release notes and context tests.

Implementation contract

@AutoConfiguration
class ReceiptGatewayAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(ReceiptGateway.class)
    ReceiptGateway receiptGateway(ReceiptGatewayProperties settings) {
        return new HttpReceiptGateway(settings.endpoint());
    }
}

Cost and verification

Condition evaluation occurs at startup, with negligible request-path cost. Maintaining a starter adds a compatibility obligation: changes to the default type or condition can alter which bean applications receive during an upgrade.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use a missing-bean condition in arbitrary user configuration and depend on incidental processing order.
  • Do not return Object from a factory when the condition needs a predictable gateway type.
  • Do not use a fallback bean to conceal invalid required credentials or endpoint settings.

title: Spring Boot ConditionalOnProperty: make optional infrastructure opt in
summary: A property condition can register a feature only for an explicit value, with absence and false kept distinct from enabled.
body:
A property condition can register a feature only for an explicit value, with absence and false kept distinct from enabled.

The absent value has meaning

A receipt replay worker should not start merely because its class is on the classpath. @ConditionalOnProperty with havingValue true and matchIfMissing false requires an explicit opt-in setting. That prevents an unreviewed deployment from running a second replay loop. Multi-instance scheduling still needs a claim or leader protocol; a property flag only controls whether a bean is registered on each instance.

Keep deployment and runtime decisions separate

The condition is evaluated while building the context. Changing a property in an external store does not automatically add or remove the worker from an already running context. Use a controlled restart or a separately designed runtime switch with defined drain behavior. Include the flag in the same deployment review as its queue, permissions and monitoring settings. Config precedence matters because command-line, environment and files may disagree about the final value.

Test the matrix

Start a minimal context with the property absent, false and true. Assert that exactly the true case registers ReceiptReplayWorker. Then test a malformed value and verify the intended behavior instead of assuming arbitrary text means enabled. A context test establishes registration; a worker integration test must separately prove idempotent claims, shutdown and retry. Configuration validation should reject a missing queue name when the feature is enabled.

Implementation contract

@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnProperty(
    prefix = "receipt.replay",
    name = "enabled",
    havingValue = "true",
    matchIfMissing = false)
class ReceiptReplayAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    ReceiptReplayWorker receiptReplayWorker(ReceiptClaimStore claims) {
        return new ReceiptReplayWorker(claims);
    }
}

Cost and verification

A disabled feature creates no worker or polling load. When enabled, each application instance evaluates the same setting and may start a worker, so database claim contention and polling volume still need explicit bounds.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume a conditional property is a live runtime toggle.
  • Do not interpret bean registration as proof that only one cluster member will run the worker.
  • Do not leave required enabled-mode settings unvalidated.

title: Spring Boot virtual threads: cheaper waiting still needs admission control
summary: Virtual threads can reduce the cost of blocking waits, but database pools, downstream capacity and JVM lifetime remain bounded resources.
body:
Virtual threads can reduce the cost of blocking waits, but database pools, downstream capacity and JVM lifetime remain bounded resources.

The switch changes thread allocation

With Java 21 or later, Spring Boot can use virtual threads for supported task execution when spring.threads.virtual.enabled is true. That can make a receipt API with many blocked I/O calls use fewer platform threads. It does not make JDBC connections, memory, rate limits or the payment provider infinite. Keep the admission limits that protect those resources. Bounded execution may need to move from a platform-thread pool to a semaphore or another explicit concurrency gate once pool-size settings no longer govern the virtual-thread executor.

Inspect the blocking path

A virtual thread can be pinned to a carrier in some blocking situations, reducing throughput instead of improving it. Measure with representative traffic and inspect JVM pinning events rather than assuming the switch helps every workload. CPU-heavy PDF rendering gains little from cheap blocking, and a database pool with 47 connections still runs at most 47 concurrent queries on that pool. Shared singleton state remains shared across virtual threads; thread count is not an isolation rule.

Keep the process alive intentionally

Virtual threads are daemon threads. A scheduler-heavy process with no other non-daemon work can exit unless the application keeps the JVM alive; spring.main.keep-alive is the Boot setting for that case. Test a worker-only deployment after startup, after an idle period and during shutdown. Compare throughput, p95 latency, database wait time and carrier pinning with the old setup. Worker drain still needs a durable retry story when the process stops.

Implementation contract

spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
spring.main.keep-alive=true

Cost and verification

Virtual threads reduce per-wait thread overhead, but each task still retains stack state and application objects. A surge of 4,700 waiting requests can exhaust a connection pool or downstream quota even when thread creation stays cheap.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not remove database or remote-call concurrency limits after enabling virtual threads.
  • Do not assume a virtual-thread switch speeds CPU-bound receipt rendering.
  • Do not ignore pinning measurements or daemon-thread process lifetime for worker-only deployments.

title: Spring Boot structured logs: stable fields without customer data
summary: A JSON log format makes events machine-readable, but field naming, correlation and data limits remain application contracts.
body:
A JSON log format makes events machine-readable, but field naming, correlation and data limits remain application contracts.

Format is only the first decision

Spring Boot can emit structured JSON on the console by selecting a supported format such as ecs. The result is easier for a collector to parse than a changing text pattern, but it does not decide which business fields belong in logs. Record event names, bounded outcomes and trace identifiers. Keep raw receipt contents, access tokens and customer contact details out of both message text and structured key-value pairs. Trace correlation joins a request across services; it does not authorize payload logging.

Preserve a small schema

Choose one service name, one environment name and stable keys for receipt action and outcome. A high-cardinality receipt ID may be acceptable in a controlled audit record, but shipping it on every debug line changes retention and access requirements. Keep the log schema versioned in the collector contract so dashboards do not break when a field is renamed. If the application supplies custom Logback or Log4j configuration, verify that it respects Boot's structured-format setting rather than assuming the property overrides a custom appender.

Test one event end to end

Generate a successful receipt issue, a rejected request and a downstream timeout. Parse the emitted lines as JSON, assert required fields and inspect every value for secret or personal-data leakage. Check collector ingestion and search by trace ID. A logger-level change can multiply line volume without changing code; runtime logger control therefore needs a bounded incident window. Metric labels should stay much narrower than searchable log fields.

Implementation contract

spring.application.name=receipt-api
logging.structured.format.console=ecs
logging.structured.ecs.service.environment=${APP_ENV:development}

Cost and verification

JSON encoding adds bytes and formatting work per event. Collector storage cost scales with event volume and retained fields; debug logging across thousands of requests can dominate the expense far more than the formatter itself.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat JSON formatting as permission to emit tokens or customer payloads.
  • Do not rename fields without checking collector queries and dashboards.
  • Do not assume custom logging configuration automatically honors the Boot format property.

title: Spring Boot SSL bundle rotation: replace certificate files with a verified handoff
summary: A named SSL bundle separates key material from server configuration; reload support still depends on the consumer and deployment sequence.
body:
A named SSL bundle separates key material from server configuration; reload support still depends on the consumer and deployment sequence.

Name the trust boundary

A receipt API serves TLS using a named PEM bundle and points server.ssl.bundle to that name. The certificate and private key live in mounted files controlled by deployment tooling, not in a repository or tutorial example. A bundle can also describe client trust material, but server identity and outbound trust have different owners. Configuration precedence determines which file locations reach the process, and HTTP authorization remains necessary after a successful TLS handshake.

Rotate both halves safely

For a compatible embedded server, reload-on-update can notice changed PEM files and refresh its TLS connector. The deployment must publish a matching certificate and key without leaving a partial pair visible to the watcher. Do not assume every client or third-party component that consumes an SslBundle reloads itself; confirm the particular consumer. Retain an overlap window when clients cache trust material, and keep a rollback pair available if the new certificate fails validation.

Verify the handshake, not just startup

Start with one test certificate, connect as a client that validates the expected issuer and name, rotate the mounted pair, then make a new connection and inspect the served certificate. Existing connections may continue under the old handshake until they close; test the new connection explicitly. A file timestamp change or successful application log entry is not proof the connector accepted the new identity. Record expiry monitoring and a failed-rotation alarm before relying on unattended renewal.

Implementation contract

spring.ssl.bundle.pem.receipt-server.keystore.certificate=file:/run/receipt-tls/tls.crt
spring.ssl.bundle.pem.receipt-server.keystore.private-key=file:/run/receipt-tls/tls.key
spring.ssl.bundle.pem.receipt-server.reload-on-update=true
server.ssl.bundle=receipt-server

Cost and verification

A reload avoids a full process restart for compatible consumers, but file watching, controlled writes and handshake tests add deployment work. A failed pair can interrupt new TLS connections until rollback or correction.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not store the private key in source control or print it during troubleshooting.
  • Do not assume every SSL bundle consumer supports live reload.
  • Do not declare rotation successful from a changed file without testing a fresh TLS handshake.

title: Spring Boot startup timeline: measure context work before extending probes
summary: Buffer startup steps to find slow initialization, then fix the owning bean or external dependency before widening readiness delays.
body:
Buffer startup steps to find slow initialization, then fix the owning bean or external dependency before widening readiness delays.

Measure the phase that is slow

A receipt service starts slowly after a new cache client and a schema check are added. A large readiness delay hides the symptom but also delays healthy replacements. Boot's BufferingApplicationStartup records startup steps for inspection; with Actuator configured, an operations-only startup endpoint can expose the timeline. This is diagnostic data about the application internals, so place it behind the same controlled management access as other operational endpoints. Startup validation should still fail promptly for a required invalid setting.

Keep the buffer bounded

The startup recorder retains a finite number of steps. Allocate enough capacity for one representative startup without making an unlimited in-memory log. Compare cold and warm starts and record the external systems contacted by slow bean constructors. A slow step may include network wait, class loading or a dependency chain; the timing alone does not prove the root cause. Early bean creation and lazy initialization change when work occurs, not necessarily how much work exists.

Test deployment readiness separately

Measure from process start to listener bind and from listener bind to readiness acceptance. A context may start while a required data migration or worker lease is still unavailable. Tune the platform startup probe from observed worst-case starts with margin, and keep liveness from killing a merely slow process. Readiness decides traffic admission; it cannot make a slow dependency fast. Re-run the timeline after each fix so an apparent gain is not just deferred work moved onto the first customer request.

Implementation contract

SpringApplication receiptApp = new SpringApplication(ReceiptApi.class);
receiptApp.setApplicationStartup(new BufferingApplicationStartup(1536));
receiptApp.run(args);

Cost and verification

Buffering retains step records during startup and adds small instrumentation work. Exposing the timeline adds an operational endpoint and access-control duty; deferring initialization may lower startup time while increasing first-request latency.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not respond to every slow startup by extending the liveness deadline.
  • Do not expose startup internals on a public management route.
  • Do not call deferred initialization a performance gain without measuring the first request.

title: Spring Data JPA assigned IDs: tell save when an entity is new
summary: An assigned primary key is not evidence that a row already exists; make new-state detection explicit before using repository save.
body:
An assigned primary key is not evidence that a row already exists; make new-state detection explicit before using repository save.

The ambiguous insert

A receipt import assigns its own stable ID before persistence. Spring Data JPA must decide whether save calls persist or merge. Without a nullable version property, a non-null ID can make a new object look existing. A merge may perform an avoidable lookup and returns a managed copy, which matters if callers keep changing the original instance. Entity lifecycle explains why this difference is observable.

Choose one state contract

A nullable @Version field lets the repository regard a null version as new, while also supporting optimistic locking. For an assigned-ID entity without a suitable version, implement Persistable and keep a transient new flag. Flip that flag with @PostPersist and @PostLoad. This is a domain decision: a reconstructed object representing an existing row must not claim it is new. Do not infer existence from an HTTP request field.

Prove both paths

In a repository integration test, save a new assigned-ID receipt and assert one row appears. Load it, change a mutable field, save again, and assert that the same row changes rather than a duplicate insert occurring. Repeat with a detached instance because that route exercises merge. Flush timing can expose SQL but does not prove a committed outcome.

Implementation contract

@Entity
class ReceiptLedger {
    @Id UUID receiptId;
    @Version Long revision;
    String status;
}
// A null revision marks a newly assigned-ID entity for persist().

Cost and verification

Choosing persist avoids a merge lookup for new records. A version column adds storage and conflict checks; correctness is more valuable than hiding one small field.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate a non-null, application-assigned ID with an existing database row.
  • Do not keep mutating the original detached object after merge returns a managed copy.
  • Do not use a primitive version field when null must mean new.

title: JPA detached merge: prevent partial requests from erasing stored fields
summary: EntityManager.merge copies detached state, so a sparse API payload must not masquerade as a complete entity snapshot.
body:
EntityManager.merge copies detached state, so a sparse API payload must not masquerade as a complete entity snapshot.

A missing field becomes a write

A client sends only a receipt status and ID. If the controller constructs a detached ReceiptEntity with the other fields left null, then calls repository save, JPA may merge the nulls into a managed copy. That makes a patch request behave like a destructive replacement. New-state detection decides persist versus merge; it does not make a partial entity safe.

Load then change allowed fields

Keep a request DTO separate from the entity. In one tenant-scoped transaction, query the row using both tenant and receipt ID, verify the expected revision, and update only fields the command permits. Dirty checking writes the changed managed entity at flush. Put invariant checks before mutation. The attached entity stays owned by this persistence context; do not hand it to a background thread or serialize it directly into an API response.

Make conflicts visible

Test a sparse request with an existing non-null customer reference and total. The update should preserve both. Test a stale revision and a cross-tenant ID; neither may change the row. A narrow JPQL update can be better for a single column if it includes the tenant and version predicates, but bulk updates bypass managed-entity synchronization.

Implementation contract

@Transactional
public ReceiptView changeStatus(UUID tenantId, UUID receiptId, long expectedRevision, String nextStatus) {
    ReceiptEntity receipt = repository.findByTenantIdAndReceiptId(tenantId, receiptId).orElseThrow();
    if (receipt.getRevision() != expectedRevision) throw new OptimisticLockingFailureException("stale receipt");
    receipt.changeStatus(nextStatus);
    return ReceiptView.from(receipt);
}

Cost and verification

Load-and-change usually needs a SELECT plus an UPDATE. It preserves field-level intent and authorization; a predicate update can use one SQL statement when its lost-update contract is explicit.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not bind a partial JSON object directly onto a managed entity.
  • Do not call merge on a sparse entity and expect null fields to be ignored.
  • Do not check ownership outside the transaction that performs the change.
