A FailureAnalyzer recognizes a specific startup exception and supplies a focused description and repair action without swallowing the failure.

Analyze one failure family

A receipt service refuses to start when its ledger schema version is unsupported. A custom analyzer can recognize that domain exception and name the incompatible version in the startup report. It must return null for unrelated failures so another analyzer or the original stack trace can handle them. The analyzer changes diagnosis, not the process outcome. Startup validation] still prevents an unsafe service from accepting traffic.

Register before the context exists

A startup failure may occur before ordinary beans are available, so registering the analyzer as an application bean is not a safe discovery strategy. Package its implementation name under the FailureAnalyzer key in META-INF/spring.factories. Keep its constructor light; avoid database queries, secrets and network calls inside error reporting. If the exception contains a password or connection string, redact that information before creating the description. The condition report] is better for missing auto-configuration than a domain-specific analyzer.

Prove both branches

Start a small application with an unsupported ledger version and capture the failure report. Check that the report names the expected version and a precise repair step, then assert startup still exits unsuccessfully. Trigger an unrelated bean creation error and confirm this analyzer does not claim it. A diagnostic that turns every exception into a generic ledger message costs more time than it saves.

final class LedgerVersionAnalyzer
        extends AbstractFailureAnalyzer<UnsupportedLedgerVersionException> {
    @Override protected FailureAnalysis analyze(
            Throwable rootFailure, UnsupportedLedgerVersionException cause) {
        return new FailureAnalysis(
            "Receipt ledger schema " + cause.schemaVersion() + " is unsupported",
            "Run the approved ledger migration before starting this service",
            rootFailure);
    }
}

An analyzer runs only on startup failure. Its operational cost is inaccurate advice or leaked secrets, not request latency.

  • Do not treat an analyzer as a recovery mechanism that permits unsafe startup.
  • Do not register it only as a normal application bean.
  • Do not echo credentials from the exception into the report.

title: Spring Boot condition report: locate the missing auto-configuration decision
summary: A condition report records why auto-configuration matched or backed off; inspect the exact condition before adding another bean or excluding a module.

A condition report records why auto-configuration matched or backed off; inspect the exact condition before adding another bean or excluding a module.

Read the decision chain

A receipt HTTP client is absent after deployment. The class might be missing, a required property might be false, or a user bean may have caused a conditional default to back off. The condition report shows positive and negative matches by configuration source. Find the failed condition for the expected auto-configuration class, then inspect the actual classpath and property value. Missing-bean defaults] and property opt-ins] cover the two common decisions.

Use a controlled diagnostic surface

Startup debug logging can print the report during local diagnosis. Actuator can expose a conditions endpoint when installed and enabled, but do not expose that endpoint on an unrestricted public management surface: it reveals class and configuration details. Capture only the relevant entry in an incident note. A missing bean error by itself does not prove that scanning failed; component scanning] and auto-configuration are different paths.

Compare before changing code

Run the same packaged artifact with the failing and healthy configuration, then compare the condition entry. Do not add an explicit bean solely to silence an exception until the reason for backoff is known. A targeted test should assert the intended bean is present when the opt-in property is true and absent when false. That proves the contract without depending on the entire text of a report, which can change across framework versions.

Logger diagnosticLog = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ReceiptApplication.class);
ConditionEvaluationReport report =
    ConditionEvaluationReport.get(context.getBeanFactory());
report.getConditionAndOutcomesBySource().entrySet().stream()
    .filter(entry -> entry.getKey().contains("ReceiptClient"))
    .forEach(entry -> diagnosticLog.info(
        "{} -> {}", entry.getKey(), entry.getValue()));

Report inspection is a diagnostic task, not a request path. Exposing it broadly increases information leakage; large reports can also be noisy without a named condition to inspect.

  • Do not infer a scan failure from every missing auto-configured bean.
  • Do not publish the conditions endpoint to anonymous clients.
  • Do not assert the full report text in a version-sensitive test.

A no-argument ConfigurationPropertiesScan scans from the annotated class package, so the library record may not be registered. A third-party object that you cannot annotate may be bound through a ConfigurationProperties bean method. The component-scan boundary] explains why importing a module does not automatically discover all its classes.

A test in the application module may see the property record because test configuration imports it, while the final packaged service does not. record ReceiptRetryProperties(int maxAttempts, Duration backoff) {}

A receipt-service patch changes controller classes but leaves the framework libraries untouched. A layered Boot archive includes an index describing layers such as dependencies, snapshot dependencies, loader code and application code. An image build can place stable library bytes before the frequently changing application layer. This improves cache reuse for transfer and rebuilds; it does not make the running Java process faster by itself. The executable jar layout] explains where the classes and nested libraries live.

Keep the index honest

Inspect the packaged archive, not only the build script. A project dependency that changes on every build may land with application code, while a snapshot library can invalidate its own layer often. Custom layer rules should follow actual change frequency and must be checked after a dependency restructure. A buildpack image] can read the layer index, but its builder and run image versions also affect cache behavior.

Measure the right cost

Build two images from the same dependency graph with only one receipt class changed. Compare layer digests, bytes pushed and deployment pull time. Then upgrade a dependency and confirm the appropriate library layer changes. A test that merely finds layers.idx proves the archive has metadata, not that the deployment pipeline actually reuses layers.

Layer metadata is small. Image size may remain similar; the benefit is fewer changed bytes sent and stored when only application code changes.

  • Do not claim layering reduces runtime latency without measuring startup separately.
  • Do not infer cache reuse solely from the presence of layers.idx.
  • Do not place frequently changing generated files in a stable dependency layer.

The receipt service image build chooses a JVM version and builder policy. The running container later receives a database address, credentials and pool limits for its deployment. }

A receipt rules document under application resources may be a visible file in an IDE and an entry inside the packaged jar in production. Calling getFile on a classpath resource assumes an ordinary filesystem path. Layering] changes image construction, not this resource-access contract.

Package the app and invoke the exact executable archive used for deployment. Read a small rules resource, then run the same feature from an IDE. Assert identical parsed values.         .getResourceAsStream("/receipt-rules.json")) {
    if (rules == null) throw new IllegalStateException("Receipt rules missing");
    receiptRules = objectMapper.readValue(rules, ReceiptRules.class);

Stream access reads only the requested bytes. Copying large bundled assets to a temporary directory adds startup I/O and storage pressure; avoid it unless the library requires a real file.

  • Do not attempt to write generated receipts into the executable jar.

title: Spring Boot process exit codes: make job failure visible to the scheduler
summary: A command-line Boot process can return a nonzero exit code for a failed business run, allowing its scheduler to distinguish failure from a clean stop.
body:
A command-line Boot process can return a nonzero exit code for a failed business run, allowing its scheduler to distinguish failure from a clean stop.

Map outcome to process status

A nightly receipt settlement may finish its Java main method even though the imported job failed. A zero process exit then tells the scheduler the run succeeded. Implement ExitCodeGenerator for the final business outcome and pass SpringApplication.exit’s result to System.exit in a one-shot process. A long-running HTTP service usually should not exit after a single request failure. Batch flow status] determines which job result should be mapped.

Avoid a false success

If a runner throws before normal shutdown, a domain exception can also carry an exit code. Test both a normal completed job and a failed job after the context closes. Several generators may exist; establish their ordering or consolidate the policy so a later nonzero code does not surprise operators. Keep the mapping small and documented in the scheduler configuration. Runner failures] are startup failures, not ordinary request errors.

Exercise the real shell contract

Launch the packaged artifact as a subprocess against a disposable input manifest. Check its numeric exit status and durable result rows. A mocked ExitCodeGenerator test can prove one method returns 47, but not that main actually passes the value to the operating system. For a retryable failure, reconcile committed chunks before the scheduler launches the same job identity again.

Implementation contract

final class SettlementExitCode implements ExitCodeGenerator {
    private final SettlementResult result;
    SettlementExitCode(SettlementResult result) { this.result = result; }
    @Override public int getExitCode() {
        return result.failed() ? 47 : 0;
    }
}
// In the one-shot main method:
System.exit(SpringApplication.exit(SpringApplication.run(ReceiptBatchApp.class, args)));

Cost and verification

Exit-code calculation is negligible. A wrong mapping can cause an unattended scheduler to skip a failed run or retry an already completed one.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not return zero after a failed batch execution.
  • Do not terminate a long-running web server for one request error.
  • Do not test only the generator while leaving the main method’s process exit unverified.

title: Spring MVC private Cache-Control: decide who may retain a receipt
summary: Cache-Control on a personalized response sets the storage boundary; a valid ETag alone does not make a tenant receipt safe for a shared cache.

Cache-Control on a personalized response sets the storage boundary; a valid ETag alone does not make a tenant receipt safe for a shared cache.

Bind the cache decision to the data

A receipt total is visible only to the authenticated tenant. A browser may keep a short-lived copy if product policy permits it, but an intermediary must not reuse the response for another user. Set a private directive on the response, and decide separately whether sensitive fields require no-store. Conditional GET] saves response bytes after authorization; it is not an authorization check.

Validate before a conditional response

A client may send If-None-Match for a receipt it no longer owns. Resolve the tenant and authorize that receipt before computing the entity tag or returning 304. Scope the tag to the representation and tenant; changing visibility or serialization must change the validator. A private cache can still retain data on a shared device, so use no-store for a receipt that must leave no local copy.

Request the same receipt as its owner and as a second tenant, including a matching If-None-Match header. The owner may receive 304 after a prior 200; the second tenant must never get a revealing 304. @GetMapping("/receipts/{receiptId}")
ResponseEntity<ReceiptView> readReceipt(
        @PathVariable UUID receiptId, Authentication authentication) {
    ReceiptView receipt = receiptService.authorizedView(authentication, receiptId);
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofMinutes(2)).cachePrivate())
        .eTag("\"" + receipt.representationVersion() + "\"")
        .body(receipt);
}

A short private cache can reduce repeated transfer and rendering. ETag calculation still costs enough to load the authorized version; no-store trades this saving for tighter data retention.

  • Do not mark tenant-specific receipts public.
  • Do not emit a 304 before checking current authorization.
  • Do not use a stable ETag when the visible representation or permissions changed.

StreamingResponseBody] is a different delivery contract.

Authorize before opening storage

Resolve the receipt through the tenant-scoped storage service, then expose only the authorized file. Do not construct a filesystem path from a client filename or ID. Return status 200 in the controller even when Range is present; the MVC resource writer decides whether the response becomes 206. Apply the appropriate private cache and download-name policy. Private caching] still matters for a partial response.

Exercise real headers

Test a normal GET, Range: bytes=0-46, an invalid range, and a second-tenant request. Check the actual Content-Range, status and selected byte count, rather than only asserting controller return values. Verify that the underlying resource stays readable until the response finishes; deleting a temporary file early can break the transfer.

Implementation contract

@GetMapping(path = "/receipts/{receiptId}/pdf", produces = "application/pdf")
ResponseEntity<Resource> download(
        @PathVariable UUID receiptId, Authentication authentication) {
    Resource pdf = receiptStorage.authorizedFile(authentication, receiptId);
    return ResponseEntity.ok() // MVC changes this to 206 for a valid Range.
        .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF)
        .cacheControl(CacheControl.noStore())
        .body(pdf);
}

Cost and verification

A range response reads and transfers only the selected bytes, but multiple tiny ranges increase request overhead. Storage still needs an efficient seekable resource and an authorization check on every request.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not return InputStreamResource for automatic range handling.
  • Do not manually set 206 on the controller ResponseEntity.
  • Do not use the request path as a storage path.

title: Spring MVC Content-Disposition: produce a safe attachment filename
summary: A download filename is presentation metadata; derive it from authorized server data and let ContentDisposition encode the header.
body:
A download filename is presentation metadata; derive it from authorized server data and let ContentDisposition encode the header.

Separate identity from a label

A client may request receipt 47 and submit an arbitrary filename in the URL. The storage lookup must use the authorized receipt identity, while the attachment label comes from a controlled server field. Restrict the label to an expected form such as receipt-47.pdf and keep its extension consistent with the response media type. Byte-range delivery] uses the same rule on every partial request.

Let the header builder encode

Content-Disposition has quoting and non-ASCII filename rules. Assemble it with ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(name, UTF_8) rather than concatenating raw user text into a header. Encoding protects header syntax, but it does not make an untrusted path component safe for storage or prevent misleading names. Normalize or reject separators, controls and unexpected extensions before building the value.

Check the client-facing result

Test ASCII and non-ASCII controlled labels and inspect the parsed Content-Disposition value. Also test a malicious submitted name; the server label should remain unchanged. A browser may choose its own saved filename despite the header, so tests should assert the response contract rather than a particular browser dialog.

Implementation contract

String attachmentName = "receipt-47.pdf"; // Derived from server metadata.
ContentDisposition attachment = ContentDisposition.attachment()
    .filename(attachmentName, StandardCharsets.UTF_8)
    .build();
return ResponseEntity.ok()
    .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, attachment.toString())
    .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF)
    .body(receiptStorage.authorizedFile(authentication, receiptId));

Cost and verification

Header construction is constant work. The expensive operation is reading the attachment; a misleading or unsafe name creates client-side confusion even when bytes are correct.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not paste a client-supplied filename into the header.
  • Do not confuse header encoding with filesystem path validation.
  • Do not advertise .pdf while returning another media type.

title: Spring MVC versioned static assets: cache immutable bytes by content
summary: A content-versioned asset URL can carry a long cache lifetime because a byte change yields a different URL; HTML and private API responses need separate policies.
body:
A content-versioned asset URL can carry a long cache lifetime because a byte change yields a different URL; HTML and private API responses need separate policies.

Version the address, not the clock

A deployed stylesheet may keep its old bytes in a browser for months. If its URL contains a content-derived version, a changed build produces a different address and can use a long public cache lifetime. A plain /assets/site.css URL cannot safely promise that lifetime across deployments. Tenant data] must not inherit this static-asset policy.

Generate URLs through the resolver

Configure a resource handler with a VersionResourceResolver, then generate links through ResourceUrlProvider or a view integration that applies the resource chain. Merely configuring the resolver does not rewrite hard-coded page URLs. If precompressed variants are served, resolver ordering matters: version the original bytes consistently. Keep HTML relatively fresh so it can point at the newly versioned asset.

Test two builds

Build with one stylesheet, capture its generated URL and response headers, then change one byte and build again. The new URL should differ, both versions should return the expected content while deployed, and the HTML should reference the current version. A CDN that purges old assets before old HTML expires can still break users.

Implementation contract

@Configuration
class AssetDelivery implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    @Override public void addResourceHandlers(ResourceHandlerRegistry registry) {
        registry.addResourceHandler("/assets/**")
            .addResourceLocations("classpath:/static/assets/")
            .setCacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofDays(365)).cachePublic())
            .resourceChain(true)
            .addResolver(new VersionResourceResolver()
                .addContentVersionStrategy("/**"));
    }
}

Cost and verification

The resource chain performs version resolution and may cache lookups. Long-lived browser and CDN copies reduce repeated asset transfer, while retaining old versioned files consumes deployment storage.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not give unversioned files a one-year public lifetime.
  • Do not assume hard-coded asset links acquire a version automatically.
  • Do not apply the asset cache rule to HTML or personalized responses.

title: Spring WebClient attributes versus Reactor Context: choose the right request scope
summary: A WebClient attribute belongs to one client request; Reactor Context follows a reactive subscription into later or nested client requests.
body:
A WebClient attribute belongs to one client request; Reactor Context follows a reactive subscription into later or nested client requests.

Keep local policy local

One receipt lookup can tag a request with a routing hint through attribute. An ExchangeFilterFunction can inspect it, but a second request created inside flatMap does not receive that attribute automatically. This is useful for a one-call option such as an audit classification. A correlation value that must reach nested requests belongs in Reactor Context at the outer subscription boundary.

Do not turn context into authority

A request attribute or context value is application metadata, not proof of user permission. The receiving service must still authenticate and authorize its own request. Keep context keys typed or centrally named to avoid collision, and avoid putting passwords or full receipt bodies there. Response ownership] remains with the code that decodes each exchange.

Test a nested call

Issue one client request that triggers another in flatMap. Assert a one-call attribute affects only the first request, then place a trace identifier in Reactor Context and assert both filters see it. Run the test without the context key too; the filter should have an explicit fallback or fail clearly rather than throwing an unexplained lookup error.

Implementation contract

WebClient receiptClient = WebClient.builder()
    .filter((request, next) -> Mono.deferContextual(context -> {
        String traceId = context.getOrDefault("receiptTraceId", "missing");
        ClientRequest tagged = ClientRequest.from(request)
            .header("X-Trace-Id", traceId).build();
        return next.exchange(tagged);
    }))
    .build();

Mono<ReceiptView> result = receiptClient.get().uri(receiptUri)
    .retrieve().bodyToMono(ReceiptView.class)
    .contextWrite(context -> context.put("receiptTraceId", "trace-47"));

Cost and verification

Context lookup and one header are small per request. The main cost is accidental metadata loss across manually started subscriptions or a security bug if context is mistaken for authorization.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect a WebClient attribute to propagate to nested requests.
  • Do not use Reactor Context as an authentication decision by itself.
  • Do not call subscribe manually in the middle of a chain and assume the original context follows.

title: Spring WebClient request audit: log route identity without payload leakage
summary: An ExchangeFilterFunction can record outbound method and approved route metadata; logging the complete URL, headers or body can leak credentials and tenant data.
body:
An ExchangeFilterFunction can record outbound method and approved route metadata; logging the complete URL, headers or body can leak credentials and tenant data.

Record a bounded event

For a receipt gateway, an outbound audit event may need the operation name, method, result category and duration. The request URL can include a token or personal identifier in its query, so omit the query and use an approved route label when paths contain IDs. Do not dump Authorization or Cookie headers. A request attribute] can carry an internal operation label for this single exchange.

Keep the response body owned

A filter that forwards next.exchange(request) can observe status without consuming the body. If it instead reads the body to print it, the caller may no longer be able to decode it and pooled buffers may remain unreleased. Capture timing around the publisher and pass the same response onward. Response ownership] explains how a filter must release a body when it terminates an exchange.

Verify safe failure paths

Use a mock HTTP server to return a success, a non-2xx response, and a connection failure. Assert one bounded event per subscription and check that secrets and query parameters never enter captured logs. Also verify the caller can still decode the body. A filter runs on subscription, so constructing a Mono alone should emit no audit event.

Implementation contract

ExchangeFilterFunction requestAudit = (request, next) -> {
    String operation = request.attribute("operation")
        .map(String::valueOf).orElse("unclassified");
    long started = System.nanoTime();
    return next.exchange(request)
        .doOnNext(response -> auditLog.info("outbound={} method={} status={} elapsedMs={}",
            operation, request.method(), response.statusCode().value(),
            Duration.ofNanos(System.nanoTime() - started).toMillis()))
        .doOnError(failure -> auditLog.warn("outbound={} method={} failed",
            operation, request.method()));
};

Cost and verification

One event per subscribed request adds log volume and formatting work. Sampling or aggregation may be needed at high request rates; logging bodies creates far greater memory, latency and privacy cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not log full URLs with query strings, credentials or personal IDs.
  • Do not consume the response body in an audit filter and then hand the empty response to the caller.
  • Do not assume a constructed but unsubscribed Mono sent a request.

title: Spring STOMP authorization: separate SEND from SUBSCRIBE permissions
summary: An authenticated WebSocket handshake does not authorize every STOMP destination; inbound MESSAGE and SUBSCRIBE frames need separate destination rules.
body:
An authenticated WebSocket handshake does not authorize every STOMP destination; inbound MESSAGE and SUBSCRIBE frames need separate destination rules.

Two frame types, two capabilities

A receipt client may send a command to an application prefix and subscribe to updates, but it must not publish directly to the broker topic. Authorization rules should allow the intended MESSAGE destination and deny client MESSAGE frames to broker prefixes. A SUBSCRIBE rule must also constrain which tenant or user queue can be observed. Handshake identity] establishes the principal; destination checks govern actions after connection.

Apply ownership to identifiers

A pattern such as /topic/tenants/{tenantId}/receipts is not safe merely because the caller is authenticated. Compare the tenantId with a verified tenant claim or domain authorization result. Keep a final deny rule for unhandled MESSAGE and SUBSCRIBE frames. Server-originated sends through SimpMessageSendingOperations follow a different path from client inbound messages. The STOMP boundary] explains that distinction.

Attack-test the matrix

Connect as two tenants. For each principal, attempt an allowed application SEND, a forbidden direct broker SEND, a permitted subscription, and a cross-tenant subscription. Assert denial at the inbound frame boundary and check that no forbidden message is broadcast. A successful HTTP handshake is not evidence that these four cases are covered.

Implementation contract

@Configuration
@EnableWebSocketSecurity
class ReceiptSocketSecurity {
    @Bean
    AuthorizationManager<Message<?>> messageAuthorization(
            MessageMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager.Builder messages) {
        messages.simpSubscribeDestMatchers("/user/queue/receipts")
            .authenticated();
        messages.simpTypeMatchers(SimpMessageType.SUBSCRIBE).denyAll();
        messages.simpDestMatchers("/topic/**", "/queue/**").denyAll();
        messages.simpDestMatchers("/app/receipts/**").authenticated();
        messages.simpTypeMatchers(SimpMessageType.MESSAGE).denyAll();
        messages.anyMessage().authenticated();
        return messages.build();
    }
}

Cost and verification

Each inbound frame incurs matcher and authorization work. Broad subscriptions can also drive high fan-out and broker memory use; authorization and slow-client budgets] address different costs.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not rely on HTTP handshake authentication as destination authorization.
  • Do not permit client MESSAGE frames to broker-owned destinations.
  • Do not use an authenticated-only rule for tenant-addressed subscriptions without checking tenant ownership.
